title: Replication: Contrastive Learning and Data Augmentation in Traffic Classification Using a Flowpic Input Representation
summary: Reproduces mini-FlowPic results and tests augmentations on additional mobile datasets.
contribution: Uncovers a data shift alongside confirmations of several original findings.
limitation: The reported drop is scenario-specific, not a universal failure of contrastive learning.
gap: More capture-aware replication across diverse traffic sources.

details.Research problem: Reproduces mini-FlowPic results and tests augmentations on additional mobile datasets.
details.Traffic unit definition: Flowpic samples summarise the first 15 seconds of a network flow. (Sections 2.2 and 4.2.1)
details.Input representation: Flowpics are two-dimensional histograms of packet size against time, without traffic direction; the study tests resolutions of 32 × 32, 64 × 64 and 1500 × 1500. The ML comparison also uses concatenated packet-size, direction and inter-arrival-time sequences. (Sections 2.2, 4.1.1 and 4.2.1; Table 4)
details.Packets / bytes: Flowpics bin packet sizes over the range 0–1500 within a 15-second observation window; the alternative ML representation uses the first 10 packets. (Sections 2.2 and 4.1.1)
details.Preprocessing / anonymisation: UCDAVIS19 is converted from CSV to Parquet without further filtering; the other datasets remove flows with fewer than 10 packets and classes with fewer than 100 samples. MIRAGE datasets additionally remove TCP ACK packets and background traffic, while the UTMOBILENET21 partitions are combined. (Section 3.4, Data curation)
details.Architecture: The study uses LeNet5 for mini-flowpics and a larger CNN for full-flowpics. SimCLR uses a feature extractor with a projection head, followed by a frozen representation and a trainable classification layer for few-shot fine-tuning. (Section 3.2; Appendix C, Listings 1–5)
details.Pretraining objective: SimCLR uses the InfoNCE contrastive objective to pull augmented views of the same sample together and separate them from negative views. (Sections 2.4 and 3.2)
details.Fine-tuning objective: A classifier layer is fine-tuned with a few labelled samples while the pretrained representation is frozen; augmentations are used only during pretraining. (Section 3.2, Training steps)
details.Pretraining datasets: SimCLR pretraining uses the UCDAVIS19 pretraining partition, initially sampled into balanced per-class subsets; an additional experiment enlarges training to the full pretraining partition. (Sections 3.4, 4 and 4.4.3)
details.Training / evaluation datasets: The study uses UCDAVIS19 with five classes, MIRAGE19 with 20 classes, MIRAGE22 with nine classes and curated UTMOBILENET21 with 14 classes. MIRAGE22 is also evaluated with a longer-flow subset; ISCX-VPN and ISCX-Tor are excluded after preliminary investigation. (Section 3.4; Table 2)
details.Split strategy: UCDAVIS19 uses five non-overlapping groups of 100 flows per class from pretraining, each with repeated 80/20 training/validation splits, and evaluates on script, human and unused pretraining flows. Replication on the other datasets specifies an 80/10/10 training/validation/test split preserving class imbalance. (Sections 4.2.1 and 4.5.1)
details.Evaluation setting: The reproduction compares supervised CNN training and SimCLR with few-shot fine-tuning across six augmentations and a no-augmentation control, with XGBoost as an ML reference. It adds ablations of resolution, dropout, projection size, augmentation pairs and training-set size, then replicates supervised augmentation comparisons on additional datasets. (Sections 3.1–3.3 and 4.1–4.5)
details.Metrics: UCDAVIS19 evaluation reports accuracy with confidence intervals; replication on the imbalanced datasets uses F1, without a stated averaging convention. Augmentation ranks are compared with a post-hoc Nemenyi test. (Sections 4.1.1, 4.3 and 4.5.1)
details.Reported results: Authors report a roughly 20% accuracy drop in some tested scenarios after uncovering a data shift.
details.Parameters: For five-class, 32 × 32 inputs, the supervised network has 61,281 parameters, SimCLR pretraining has 68,842 or 75,376 depending on projection size, and the fine-tuning architecture has 51,297. (Appendix C, Listings 1–5)
details.Memory: For 32 × 32 inputs, architecture printouts estimate total memory of 0.36 MB for supervised learning, 0.39 MB for the smaller SimCLR projection, 0.42 MB for the larger projection and 0.33 MB for fine-tuning. (Appendix C, Listings 1–5)
details.Reproducibility: No experiments independently rerun for this explorer.
details.Leakage / shortcut risks: Inspection of the reference repository finds that its loader mixes UCDAVIS19 partitions and includes test flows in training; the authors also identify distribution shift in the human partition. They exclude ISCX datasets after noting insufficient viable flows and published concerns about exploitable dataset bias. (Section 3.4, Reproducibility; Section 4.2.3; Appendix D)
details.Deployment limitations: Flowpics require observing multiple seconds of traffic, which can delay classification and limit their suitability for prioritisation, scheduling and shaping. (Section 2.2, Related work)
details.Version notes: The reference repository differs from the published architecture, activation functions, dropout and learning-rate scheduling, preventing faithful reproduction from that code. The original authors also clarified that they combined the pretraining and script partitions, whereas this study initially treated them separately. (Appendix D; Section 4.2.1, footnote 10)
details.Hardware: Experiments run on Linux servers equipped with multiple NVIDIA Tesla V100 GPUs. (Section 3.3)
details.Measurement scope: Memory figures are torchsummary architecture estimates; reported experiment durations describe modelling runs rather than packet-processing measurements. (Section 4.2.2; Appendix C, Listings 1–5)

title: SoK: Pragmatic Assessment of Machine Learning for Network Intrusion Detection
summary: Evaluates the operational value of ML-based network intrusion detection.
contribution: Studies many configurations, adversarial scenarios and four hardware platforms.
limitation: Hardware-specific findings should not become universal model rankings.
gap: Reproducible deployment decisions including operational error costs.

details.Research problem: Evaluates the operational value of ML-based network intrusion detection.
details.Traffic unit definition: Traffic is represented as high-level NetFlow records summarizing communications between two endpoints. (Section 2.1; Appendix A.1)
details.Input representation: Models take either a Complete feature set using all features generated by the respective flow exporter, or an Essential feature set consisting of approximately half the features including basic flow metadata. (Section D.4)
details.Preprocessing / anonymisation: Plain IP addresses and network ports are removed to prevent shortcut learning, with ports converted to their corresponding IANA category. (Section D.4)
details.Architecture: Six pipeline designs are evaluated (binary BD, multiclass MD, binary-to-multiclass cascade BMD, and ensembles ED-o, ED-v, ED-s) across four classification algorithms: Decision Trees, Random Forests, Logistic Regression, and Histogram Gradient Boosting. (Section 6.1; Section D.6)
details.Pretraining objective: NA — no pretraining stage recorded for this contribution
details.Pretraining datasets: NA — no pretraining stage recorded for this contribution
details.Training / evaluation datasets: Five flow datasets are used: CTU13 (Argus), NB15 (Zeek), UF-NB15 (nProbe), CICIDS17 (FlowMeter fixed version), and GTCS (FlowMeter). (Section 6.1; Table 4)
details.Split strategy: The test set E is composed of 20% of samples per class randomly chosen from the dataset D. Training set T evaluates four availability levels (80%, 40%, 15%, or 100 samples per class) over 100 to 1,000 random trials for static evaluation, plus a chronological split using the initial samples for training and the final 20% for testing. (Section 6.1; Section D.3)
details.Evaluation setting: The benchmark evaluates four machine learning algorithms across six architectural detector pipelines, two feature sets, five datasets, four data budget regimes, and both static and temporal splits under known, unknown, and adversarial attack scenarios. (Section 6.1)
details.Metrics: Evaluation measures true positive rate (tpr), false positive rate (fpr), training and testing runtimes, and accuracy (Acc) calculated exclusively on malicious classes for multiclass setups. (Section E.3)
details.Reported results: NA — not extracted
details.Reproducibility: No experiments independently rerun for this explorer.
details.Leakage / shortcut risks: To eliminate experimental bias and shortcut artefacts, the authors stripped IP addresses and replaced raw ports with IANA functional categories, addressed sample composition skew, and tested time-ordered splits. (Section D.3; Section D.4)
details.Deployment limitations: Key operational hurdles identified by the authors include the uniqueness and dynamic evolution of individual networks, the presence of adaptive adversaries, and the difficulty of interpreting complex machine learning decisions. (Section 3.2; Section 7.1)
details.Version notes: Section 6.1 lists scarce training data availability as 20% of D, whereas Section D.3 specifies it as 15% of D (one fifth of the non-test remainder). (Section 6.1; Section D.3)
details.Hardware: Evaluations span six platforms: an Intel Xeon W-2195 with 36 cores and 256 GB RAM, an Intel Core i7-10750HQ workstation with 32 GB RAM, an Intel Core i5-4670 desktop with 8 GB RAM, an Intel Core i5-430M laptop with 8 GB RAM, a 4-core 8 GB RAM downclocked virtual machine, and a Raspberry Pi 4B with 2 GB RAM. (Section D.2)
details.Measurement scope: Runtime covers standalone training duration on partition T and complete batch inference duration across all samples in test partition E. (Section E.3)

summary: Models heterogeneous traffic as a generative pretraining problem.

details.Architecture: GPT-2 auto-regressive Transformer. (Section 3.1)
details.Pretraining objective: auto-regressive next token prediction. (Section 3.1)
details.Fine-tuning objective: traffic understanding reformulated as generation with prompts. (Section 3.2)

details.Evaluation setting: compared with ET-BERT and GPT-2 on packet and flow levels. (Section 4.1)

details.Reported results: Generation: NetGPT and GPT-2 reach JSD around 0.1; NetGPT has the best average and lowers JSD on ISXW by about 50% relative to GPT-2. (Section 4.3; Table 3)

title: Lens: A Knowledge-Guided Foundation Model for Network Traffic
summary: Introduces knowledge-guided span prediction and context-aware fine-tuning.
contribution: Formulates classification as closed-ended generation to extend label spaces.
limitation: Extension with labelled adaptation is not zero-shot unknown-class recognition.
gap: Assess calibration and cost for generative classification.

details.Research problem: Introduces knowledge-guided span prediction and context-aware fine-tuning.
details.Traffic unit definition: Flow-level traffic segmented with SplitCap by the standard 5-tuple, using the first 34 packets for classification, and packet-level traffic (one packet sampled per flow) for generation. (Section 4; Appendix A.1)
details.Input representation: Text-like sequences parsed via Tshark including network, transport, and application metadata followed by a 12-byte hexadecimal payload, tokenised using a Byte-level Byte Pair Encoding tokenizer alongside task context. (Section 3.1; Appendix A.1)
details.Packets / bytes: Classification uses the first 34 packets per flow (up to a 1,500 token limit), appending a 12-byte hexadecimal application payload per packet. (Appendix A.1)
details.Preprocessing / anonymisation: Flows are extracted using SplitCap, parsed with Tshark, and all source and destination IP addresses are replaced with placeholder tokens (<SIP> and <DIP>). (Appendix A.1)
details.Architecture: T5-v1.1-base encoder-decoder architecture implemented via TurboT5, comprising 12 encoder layers, 12 decoder layers, 12 attention heads of dimension 64, hidden dimension 768, MLP hidden dimension 2048, and Gated-GeLU activation. (Section 4; Appendix E, Table 17)
details.Pretraining objective: Knowledge-Guided Masked Span Prediction (KG-MSP) which masks metadata and payload fields based on network importance, combined with natural language context span masking at an overall 15% mask ratio. (Section 3.2; Section 3.2.1)
details.Fine-tuning objective: Closed-ended text generation using context-aware finetuning, with decoding output space constrained to valid label candidates via a prefix trie. (Section 3.3)
details.Pretraining datasets: A 60% stratified flow sample from ISCX-VPN, ISCX-Tor, USTC-TFC-2016, CIC-DoHBrw-2020, and CIC-IoT-2023, coupled with the mini C4 natural language corpus for tokenizer training. (Section 4; Appendix A.2, Table 10)
details.Training / evaluation datasets: Six datasets comprising 12 classification tasks: ISCX-VPN (tasks 1 to 3; 2, 6, 16 classes), ISCX-Tor / USTC-TFC-2016 (tasks 4 and 5; 7 and 16 classes), Cross Platform Android (tasks 6 and 7; 209 and 3 classes), Cross Platform iOS (tasks 8 and 9; 196 and 3 classes), CIC-DoHBrw-2020 (task 10; 5 classes), and CIC-IoT-2023 (tasks 11 and 12; 2 and 7 classes). (Section 4.1; Appendix A.3, Table 11)
details.Split strategy: Stratified sampling of 60% of flows for pretraining on coarse categories; finetuning randomly selects roughly 10k flows per dataset (or 15% for Cross Platform Android and 26% for Cross Platform iOS). (Section 4; Appendix A.2, Table 10)
details.Metrics: Accuracy and Macro F1 score for classification; Jensen-Shannon Divergence and Total Variation Distance for generation. (Section 4)
details.Reported results: Lens achieved an average accuracy of 96.33% across all 12 classification tasks, reaching 0.9942 accuracy / 0.9870 macro F1 on Task 1, 0.8979 / 0.8893 on Task 2, 0.8406 / 0.8137 on Task 3, 0.9692 / 0.8120 on Task 4, 0.9538 / 0.9676 on Task 5, 0.9660 / 0.8847 on Task 6, 0.9960 / 0.9898 on Task 7, 0.9752 / 0.9492 on Task 8, 0.9951 / 0.9951 on Task 9, 0.9963 / 0.9610 on Task 10, 0.9877 / 0.9870 on Task 11, and 0.9878 / 0.6802 on Task 12. (Section 4.1, Table 2 and Table 3)
details.Reproducibility: No experiments independently rerun for this explorer.
details.Leakage / shortcut risks: Pretraining stratification uses coarse dataset-level categories without downstream application labels to prevent label leakage, and IP addresses are masked to avert identifier leakage. (Section 4; Appendix A.1)
details.Deployment limitations: NA — not extracted
details.Version notes: First posted February 2024; latest reviewed revision January 2026 changes title and byline. The abstract gives 96.33% average accuracy over the 12 tasks; the introduction gives 96.31%. (Abstract; Section 1)
details.Code availability: Latest abstract promises code upon publication; public release not verified.

title: NetBench: A Large-Scale and Comprehensive Network Traffic Benchmark Dataset for Foundation Models
summary: Aggregates seven public datasets into 15 classification and five generation tasks.
contribution: Standardises evaluation and highlights preprocessing-related leakage risk.
limitation: A benchmark still inherits collection and label limitations of its source datasets.
gap: Add temporal and organisation-disjoint validation tracks.

details.Research problem: Aggregates seven public datasets into 15 classification and five generation tasks.
details.Traffic unit definition: Both flows and single packets are used; flows are extracted as packets sharing distinct combinations of IP addresses, port numbers and protocols, and every dataset is offered at both flow level and packet level. (Section 3.1 (Data Pre-Processing, Data Segmentation))
details.Input representation: Anonymised packets (header and payload) are converted to hexadecimal, then the WordPiece algorithm segments the hex into 4-digit blocks with symbols </s>, <head> and <pkt> marking sequence ends, header separation and packet demarcation; flow-level input concatenates packets with these markers. (Section 3.1 (Data Standardization); Figure 2)
details.Preprocessing / anonymisation: PCAP files are first segmented into distinct training, validation and testing sets before flow extraction, and each packet is anonymised by masking source and destination IP addresses and port numbers, replaced with 0. (Section 3.1 (Data Pre-Processing))
details.Architecture: Recorded method family: Evaluation & surveys. Architecture details: NA — not extracted.
details.Pretraining objective: NA — no pretraining stage recorded for this contribution
details.Pretraining datasets: NA — no pretraining stage recorded for this contribution
details.Training / evaluation datasets: Seven public datasets: ISCXVPN 2016, ISCXTor 2016, USTC-TFC 2016, Cross-Platform (Android) 2020, Cross-Platform (iOS) 2020, CIRA-CIC-DoHBrw 2020 and CIC IoT Dataset 2023, yielding 15 classification tasks with 2 to 212 labels and 5 generation tasks over consecutive packets from the same datasets; totals are 2,952,302 flows and 69,799,192 packets. (Abstract; Table 1)
details.Split strategy: Training, validation and testing split at a ratio of 8:1:1; PCAP files are segmented into distinct sets before flows and packets are extracted, so highly correlated same-flow packets cannot appear in both training and testing data. (Section 4.1 (Dataset); Section 3.1 (Data Pre-Processing))
details.Evaluation setting: Eight major SOTA open-source models are assessed: classifiers DataNet, FS-Net, BiLSTM_ATTN, DeepPacket, TSCRNN, ET-BERT and YaTC, plus generative models STAN and NetShare; ET-BERT and YaTC use released pre-trained weights fine-tuned on the entire prepared training set, FS-Net is evaluated at flow level only, other classifiers at both levels, and generative models use randomly sampled consecutive packets. (Section 4.1 (SOTA Models))
details.Metrics: Classification tasks are scored with Accuracy and Macro F1 Score; generation tasks are scored with Jensen-Shannon Divergence and Total Variation Distance. (Section 4.1 (Evaluation metrics))
details.Reported results: The benchmark's headline finding is that foundation models ET-BERT and YaTC significantly outperform the traditional deep learning classifiers across the classification tasks (YaTC packet-level reaches 0.9984 accuracy and 0.9961 F1 on Task 1), while traditional methods bias towards dominant classes; NetShare generates IP addresses and port numbers better, STAN generates packet length better. (Section 4.2; Tables 3-5)
details.Reproducibility: No experiments independently rerun for this explorer.
details.Leakage / shortcut risks: The authors report that randomly splitting packets of the same flow across training and testing causes data leakage because same-flow packets are strongly correlated, and they flag ET-BERT and YaTC's packet-level processing as facing this risk; NetBench avoids it by splitting PCAPs before extraction. (Section 1; Section 2; Section 3.1)
details.Deployment limitations: The authors state that foundation models' input length constraints cause over-long input flows to be truncated, keeping flow-level foundation models from surpassing packet-level ones on some tasks; they add that longer input length is needed for increasingly complex traffic and that very few foundation models investigate traffic generation. (Section 4.2; Section 5 (Conclusion))
details.Version notes: Model counts are internally inconsistent: the abstract says eight SOTA classification models plus two generative models, while Section 4.1 counts 8 major SOTA open-source models yet lists seven classification models and two generative models. (Abstract; Section 4.1)
details.Measurement scope: Use only the setup stated in the cited results; unextracted conditions remain NA.

title: TrafficGPT: Breaking the Token Barrier for Efficient Long Traffic Analysis and Generation
summary: Uses generative pretraining and linear attention for longer traffic sequences.
contribution: Extends sequence capacity to 12,032 tokens in the reported design.
limitation: A longer context can increase collection latency even if model attention is efficient.
gap: Measure end-to-end latency and protocol-valid generation.

details.Research problem: Uses generative pretraining and linear attention for longer traffic sequences.
details.Traffic unit definition: A traffic flow is defined by the network five-tuple, representing a sequence of packets that share identical source and destination IP addresses, ports, and protocols. (Section III-B)
details.Input representation: Each flow is converted into a reversible sequence of 260 discrete tokens, structured as packet start tokens, link-type tokens, 8-byte exponential time interval tokens, hexadecimal byte tokens for header and payload, and an end token. (Section III-B)
details.Packets / bytes: Pre-training accommodates maximum token sequence lengths of 3,072 or 12,032 tokens, whereas fine-tuning evaluations predominantly use a maximum token length of 256. (Section IV-A; Section IV-B)
details.Preprocessing / anonymisation: Packets from protocols other than TCP or UDP (such as ARP and DHCP) are discarded. In classification evaluations, MAC addresses, IP addresses, and port information are stripped to avoid shortcut learning. (Section IV-A; Section IV-B)
details.Architecture: TrafficGPT is an auto-regressive model using linear attention with local attention and reversible residual layers. It has 24 layers, a hidden dimension of 512, 12 attention heads, 8 local attention heads with a local window of 256, an embedding dimension of 256, and token shifting. (Section III-A; Section IV-A)
details.Pretraining objective: Auto-regressive self-supervised language modelling trained to predict the next token via cross-entropy loss. (Section III-C)
details.Fine-tuning objective: A classification task where a [cls] token is prepended to the flow tokens and the model predicts the class label at the next output position. (Section III-E)
details.Pretraining datasets: A compilation of five public datasets totalling 189 GB: ISCXTor2016, USTCTFC2016, ISCXVPN2016, DoHBrw2020, and CICIoT2022. (Section IV-A)
details.Training / evaluation datasets: Evaluations are performed on Cross-Platform iOS (196 classes), Cross-Platform Android (215 classes), ISCX-VPN-App (13 classes), and USTC-TFC (20 classes). (Section IV-B)
details.Split strategy: Flow-level partition where 99% of flows are allocated to pre-training and 1% are reserved for testing. (Section IV-A)
details.Metrics: Macro F1-score and accuracy (AC) for classification; Jensen-Shannon Divergence (JSD) for packet headers and flow features in generation. (Section IV-B; Table I; Section IV-C)
details.Reported results: TrafficGPT(12k) achieved Macro F1-scores of 0.9863 on Cross-Platform (iOS), 0.9498 on Cross-Platform (Android), 1.0000 on ISCX-VPN-App, and 0.9877 on USTC-TFC. (Section IV-B; Table I)
details.Reproducibility: No experiments independently rerun for this explorer.
details.Leakage / shortcut risks: Models may exploit dataset shortcuts such as IP addresses or MAC addresses; hence, these fields were removed during preprocessing. (Section IV-B)
details.Deployment limitations: The model operates only on individual TCP and UDP flows, missing multi-flow correlations, and exhibits anomalies generating encrypted traffic, such as malformed TLS Client Hello packets. (Section IV-C; Section V)

details.Research problem: Splits inference between a small in-network model and a larger endpoint model.
details.Traffic unit definition: Packet, flow, aggregate, and file granularity. (Section I)

details.Preprocessing / anonymisation: Feature selection by ML importance score; Jane Street features anonymized; quantization and normalization for fixed-point encoding. (Section VI; Section VIII-A2; Section V-C)
details.Architecture: Match-Action pipeline on RMT/PISA-based programmable switches (Intel Tofino, NetFPGA SUME). (Section V)
details.Pretraining objective: NA — no pretraining stage recorded for this contribution
details.Pretraining datasets: NA — no pretraining stage recorded for this contribution

details.Metrics: Misclassification rate, F1 score, accuracy, error rate. (Section VIII-G)

title: One Train for Two Tasks: An Encrypted Traffic Classification Framework Using Supervised Contrastive Learning
summary: Uses supervised contrastive learning and byte-graph augmentations.
contribution: Shares representations across packet-level and flow-level tasks.
limitation: The reported FLOP advantage needs input and task alignment with ET-BERT.
gap: Measure end-to-end efficiency and cross-dataset stability.

details.Research problem: Uses supervised contrastive learning and byte-graph augmentations.
details.Traffic unit definition: Dual packet-level and flow-level classification; samples are bidirectional flows capped at 15 packets, with ISCX-Tor flows additionally divided into 60-second non-overlapping blocks. (Section 4.1.2; Section 4.1.3)
details.Input representation: Byte-level traffic graphs (TFE-GNN style) where nodes are byte values and edges encode semantic correlation between bytes; packet vectors are fused into a flow embedding by an LSTM. (Section 3.2.1; Section 3.2.2)
details.Packets / bytes: At most the first 15 packets of a flow are used; packet bytes (after Ethernet/IP/port removal) form the byte-level traffic graph, with header and payload graphs perturbed separately in ablations. (Section 4.1.2; Table 3)
details.Preprocessing / anonymisation: SplitCap extracts bidirectional flows; ISCX-Tor flows are enriched by 60-second non-overlapping blocks; flows without payload or surpassing length 10000 are filtered; bad and retransmission packets removed; Ethernet header, IP addresses and port numbers removed. (Section 4.1.2)
details.Architecture: A shared TFE-GNN graph encoder produces packet vectors, an LSTM fuses them into flow vectors, and PReLU MLP heads classify both levels; views are augmented by node, edge and packet dropping (ratios 0.05, 0.1, 0.6) with temperature 0.07. Two modules: dual-level contrastive learning and cross-level multi-task learning. (Section 3.1; Section 3.4; Section 4.1.3)
details.Pretraining objective: NA — not extracted
details.Fine-tuning objective: End-to-end joint objective in a single training (no pretraining): L = L_PCLS + L_FCLS + alpha*L_PCL + beta*L_FCL, combining cross-entropy classification losses at packet and flow levels with supervised contrastive losses weighted by alpha, beta in [0,1]. (Section 3.4)
details.Pretraining datasets: NA — not extracted
details.Training / evaluation datasets: ISCX VPN-nonVPN (ISCX-VPN and ISCX-nonVPN) divided into six categories and ISCX Tor-nonTor (ISCX-Tor and ISCX-nonTor) into eight; all experiments run independently on the four datasets, with statistics in Appendix E. (Section 4.1.1)
details.Split strategy: Flow-level stratified sampling into 9:1 train:test by number of traffic flows for all datasets; packets of the flow-level train/test sets serve directly as packet-level train/test, inheriting their flow's label. (Section 4.1.2)
details.Metrics: Overall Accuracy (AC), Precision (PR), Recall (RC) and Macro F1-score (F1); averaging for PR/RC is not stated. (Section 4.1.3)
details.Reported results: Authors report approximately 1/14 of ET-BERT FLOPs in their setting.
details.Parameters: No absolute parameter count is stated; Figure 3(b) (in millions) shows CLE-TFE's parameters only slightly above TFE-GNN due to the added packet-level classification head, and far below ET-BERT. (Section 4.5; Figure 3(b))
details.FLOPs: About 1/14 of ET-BERT's FLOPs; smaller than TFE-GNN because a shorter flow length suffices, with augmentation and contrastive loss adding negligible extra cost. (Abstract; Section 4.5)
details.Reproducibility: No experiments independently rerun for this explorer.
details.Leakage / shortcut risks: The authors remove IP addresses and port numbers to eliminate potential interference such fields could otherwise introduce; no other leakage or shortcut tests are reported. (Section 4.1.2)
details.Deployment limitations: The graph augmentation is non-trainable and may give sub-optimal results; hard negative samples are not optimised sufficiently; jointly optimising both tasks in one training introduces trade-offs between the two tasks. (Section 6; Section 4.2)
details.Version notes: NA — not extracted
details.Hardware: NVIDIA RTX 3080 GPU, implemented in PyTorch and Deep Graph Library; results are means over five runs. (Section 4.1.3)
details.Measurement scope: Efficiency numbers cover only FLOPs and parameter counts (offline comparison with ET-BERT, TFE-GNN and CLE-TFE w/o AUG&CL); no throughput, latency or memory measurements are reported. (Section 4.5)

title: Characterizing User Platforms for Video Streaming in Broadband Networks
summary: Identifies device and software platforms from TCP/QUIC and TLS handshakes.
contribution: Deploys a 62-attribute pipeline in a campus network over four months.
limitation: Provider-specific handshake differences may change with software versions.
gap: Longitudinal robustness of handshake fingerprints.

details.Research problem: Identifies device and software platforms from TCP/QUIC and TLS handshakes.
details.Traffic unit definition: Per-video streaming flow, classified using handshake messages from the initial connection establishment phase. (Section 2)
details.Input representation: A total of 62 attributes derived from TCP/QUIC and TLS ClientHello handshake fields, consisting of 20 numerical, 31 categorical (mapped to integers or presence flags), and 11 list fields encoded as fixed-length positional vectors. (Section 4.2; Table 2)
details.Packets / bytes: Classification uses handshake messages extracted from the first fewer than 5 packets of the connection setup. (Section 3.2.2)
details.Preprocessing / anonymisation: Packets are parsed to identify video flows by port number and TLS SNI, then split into handshake packets for classification and data packets for telemetry, with campus traffic analyzed without user identities. (Section 4.1)
details.Architecture: A bank of twelve Random Forest classifiers (three per streaming provider) predicting composite user platform, device type, and software agent, falling back to separate predictions if composite confidence is below 80%. (Section 4.1)
details.Pretraining objective: NA — no pretraining stage recorded for this contribution
details.Pretraining datasets: NA — no pretraining stage recorded for this contribution
details.Training / evaluation datasets: A lab dataset of nearly 10,000 video flows across 30 user platforms for YouTube, Netflix, Disney+, and Amazon Prime Video; an open-set home dataset with over 2,000 flows; and a 4-month campus deployment capturing over 100 million video flows. (Section 3.1; Section 4.3.2; Section 5.2)
details.Split strategy: 10-fold cross-validation on the lab dataset, supplemented by open-set evaluation on a distinct home network dataset. (Section 4.3.1; Section 4.3.2)
details.Evaluation setting: Benchmarked against six state-of-the-art methods ([6], [14], [28], [40], [53], [55]) adapted to handle QUIC Initial packets, extract flow-level TLS ClientHello features, and predict user platforms. (Section 4.3.4; Table 6)
details.Metrics: Overall classification accuracy and prediction confidence (probability of the predicted class). (Section 4.1; Section 4.3.1)
details.Reported results: Paper reports >96% classification accuracy and observes 100+ million video streams over four months.
details.Throughput: A peak real-time processing throughput of 20 Gbps and over 1,000 concurrent video flows during live campus deployment. (Section 4.3.3)
details.Reproducibility: No experiments independently rerun for this explorer.
details.Deployment limitations: Performance degrades over time due to concept drift caused by software and firmware updates, requiring periodic retraining, while novel streaming services and platforms require new ground truth data collection. (Section 5.3)
details.Version notes: NA — not extracted
details.Hardware: A commodity blade server equipped with an 8-core Intel Xeon E5-2620 CPU, 64 GB DDR4 RAM, and two 10 Gbps network interfaces. (Section 5.1)
details.Measurement scope: Live end-to-end pipeline covering packet parsing, attribute generation, classification, and telemetry logging using DPDK, NFF-Go, Golang, and scikit-learn. (Section 5.1)

title: TrafficFormer: An Efficient Pre-trained Model for Traffic Data
summary: Adds fine-grained pretraining and traffic-field augmentation to a traffic Transformer.
contribution: Uses same-origin, direction and flow structure to strengthen representation learning.
limitation: Removing explicit identifiers does not guarantee removal of all implicit flow identifiers.
gap: Capture-aware evaluation of protocol understanding and shortcut resistance.

details.Research problem: Adds fine-grained pretraining and traffic-field augmentation to a traffic Transformer.
details.Traffic unit definition: Flow (5-tuple) split by SplitCap; pre-training structures traffic as bursts of consecutive same-direction packets.
details.Input representation: Hexadecimal packet bytes tokenised as bigrams with BPE; first 5 packets per flow in fine-tuning.
details.Packets / bytes: 64 bytes per packet after the Ethernet layer; first 5 packets per flow; maximum sequence length 512.
details.Preprocessing / anonymisation: Flows under 2 KB or 3 packets and classes under 10 flows removed; at most 500 flows per class. IP, port, TCP timestamps and TLS timestamps/SNI processed with field augmentation to prevent shortcuts.
details.Architecture: Transformer encoder: 12 layers, 12 attention heads, encoding dimension 768.
details.Pretraining objective: Two tasks trained jointly: Masked Burst Modelling (cross-entropy over masked tokens) and Same Origin-Direction-Flow, a 5-class burst-pair classification (cross-entropy). Total loss = λ·loss_MBM + loss_SODF with λ = 0.1.
details.Pretraining datasets: About 20 GB, over 600,000 flows: ISCX-NonVPN (non-VPN portion), CICMalAnal2017 (2017 benign software traffic) and Browser (Table 3).
details.Training / evaluation datasets: Six fine-tuning tasks: Cross-Platform Android (197 classes) and iOS (190), CSTNET-TLS 1.3 (120), ISCX-VPN Service (6) and App (11), USTC-TFC (14) (Table 4).
details.Metrics: Accuracy, precision, recall and F1; per-class one-vs-rest values averaged across classes.
details.Reported results: TrafficFormer w/ EA F1: Cross-Platform Android 0.6167, iOS 0.4689, CSTNET-TLS 1.3 0.8338, ISCX-VPN Service 0.9580, App 0.7129, USTC-TFC 0.9830 (Tables 5–7).

title: The Sweet Danger of Sugar: Debunking Representation Learning for Encrypted Traffic Classification
summary: Reassesses five pretrained traffic models under controlled splits and feature interventions.
contribution: Tests implicit identifiers, frozen embeddings and a header-focused Pcap-Encoder.
limitation: Findings are specific to tested checkpoints, tasks and splits; revised models need new tests.
gap: A shared benchmark that separates pretraining value from split shortcuts.

details.Research problem: Reassesses five pretrained traffic models under controlled splits and feature interventions.
details.Traffic unit definition: Packet classification and bidirectional flow classification; a flow comprises packets sharing the same 5-tuple, including both client and server packets. (Section 4.2, Downstream task)
details.Input representation: Packet bytes are converted into space-separated hexadecimal words and passed through the original T5 tokenizer. (Section 3.4, Phase 1)
details.Packets / bytes: Pcap-Encoder represents individual packets; flow classification uses majority voting over the first 5 packets. (Sections 3.4 and 6.2)
details.Preprocessing / anonymisation: The benchmark filters extraneous protocols, preserves test class distributions and avoids minimum packet or flow size filters. Pcap-Encoder pretraining randomises IP addresses and TTL values to discourage memorisation. (Section 4.1, Data cleaning and Sampling; Section 3.4, footnote 6; Appendix A.4)
details.Architecture: Pcap-Encoder uses T5-base with a mean pooling bottleneck and a two-layer MLP classification head with ReLU activation. (Section 3.4; Figure 2)
details.Pretraining objective: Sequential packet reconstruction using token cross-entropy, followed by question answering about protocol header fields and computations. (Section 3.4, Phases 1 and 2; Appendix A.1.3; Table 10)
details.Fine-tuning objective: Separate downstream classifiers are trained for each task, using binary cross-entropy or softmax according to the number of classes. (Section 3.4, Downstream classifiers)
details.Pretraining datasets: MAWI, UNSW-NB15 and a freshly collected campus trace are used for both pretraining phases. (Section 3.4, Phases 1 and 2)
details.Training / evaluation datasets: ISCX-VPN supplies VPN-binary, VPN-service and VPN-app tasks with 2, 6 and 16 classes; USTC-TFC supplies binary and application tasks with 2 and 20 classes. CSTN-TLS1.3 supplies TLS-120 website classification with 120 classes. (Section 4.1; Table 2)
details.Split strategy: The principal protocol uses a random per-flow 7:1 training/test split, balances training classes by undersampling and applies 3-fold cross-validation within training. A comparison protocol uses a random per-packet 8:1:1 training/validation/test split. (Section 5, Downstream task evaluation)
details.Evaluation setting: ET-BERT, YaTC, NetMamba, TrafficFormer and netFound are evaluated alongside Pcap-Encoder and shallow baselines, using shared splits and original pretrained checkpoints. Packet and flow classification compare frozen and unfrozen encoders, with per-flow and per-packet splitting examined for packet classification. (Section 5; Sections 6.1 and 6.2; Tables 3–9)
details.Metrics: Accuracy and macro-averaged F1-score, with the latter giving equal weight to each class. (Section 4.2, Performance metrics; Table 3)
details.Reported results: With frozen encoders and per-flow splitting, Pcap-Encoder achieves packet accuracy/macro F1 of 83.5%/71.0% on VPN-app and 71.0%/63.7% on TLS-120. Flow classification achieves 69.2%/62.2% and 71.3%/68.1%, respectively. (Tables 3 and 9; Sections 6.1 and 6.2)
details.Reproducibility: No experiments independently rerun for this explorer.
details.Leakage / shortcut risks: Per-packet splitting lets models associate test packets with training flows through explicit identifiers and implicit identifiers such as TCP sequence numbers, acknowledgement numbers and timestamps. The authors test these shortcuts by randomising the implicit identifiers and also identify pretraining/downstream dataset reuse as a leakage risk. (Sections 3.2, 4.1 and 6.1; Table 6; Figure 5)
details.Deployment limitations: Pcap-Encoder's complexity and performance comparable to shallow models call its practicality into question; it is the second slowest evaluated model at both training and inference. (Sections 6.3 and 8)
details.Version notes: Criticism of netFound concerns the earlier model, not the May 2026 v5 revision.
details.Hardware: Experiments use an HPC cluster equipped with NVIDIA Tesla V100 SXM2 GPUs. (Section 6, opening paragraph)
details.Measurement scope: Efficiency compares training and inference time for completing cross-validation on VPN-app with per-flow splitting, normalised to Random Forest. (Section 6.3; Figure 6)

title: Demystifying Network Foundation Models
summary: Studies embedding geometry, domain-feature alignment and causal sensitivity.
contribution: Diagnoses what four network models encode beyond downstream accuracy.
limitation: Embedding probes measure selected properties rather than every operational task.
gap: Build protocol-sensitive representations that transfer to new contexts.

details.Research problem: Studies embedding geometry, domain-feature alignment and causal sensitivity.
details.Traffic unit definition: The intrinsic evaluation operates on flow embeddings extracted from each model's final encoder layer. (Section 3.1, Methodology)
details.Input representation: The framework analyses frozen encoder embeddings and compares them with CICFlowMeter features; causal tests additionally use embeddings from perturbed traffic. (Sections 3.2 and 3.3; Figure 1)
details.Preprocessing / anonymisation: Datasets are processed into flow records using the original models' data processing scripts, preserving their original input pipelines. Protocol perturbations modify semantically meaningful packet features rather than applying identical token changes across models. (Sections 4.1, 4.2 and 4.5)
details.Architecture: Recorded method family: Evaluation & surveys. Architecture details: NA — not extracted.
details.Pretraining objective: NA — no pretraining stage recorded for this contribution
details.Fine-tuning objective: A linear classifier is trained on frozen raw or normalised embeddings for downstream classification; logistic regression probes distinguish synthetic network contexts. (Sections 3.3 and 4.3; Appendix D)
details.Pretraining datasets: NA — no pretraining stage recorded for this contribution
details.Training / evaluation datasets: Evaluation uses Android Crossmarket, CIC-IDS2017, CIC-APT-IIoT24, CAIDA and MAWI. NetReplica additionally generates synthetic contexts varying congestion control, active queue management and cross-traffic. (Sections 4.2 and 4.6; Table 1; Appendices B and J)
details.Evaluation setting: Unmodified public pretrained checkpoints of YaTC, ET-BERT, netFound and NetMamba are evaluated through frozen embedding geometry, alignment with expert features and causal sensitivity tests. Tests include protocol-feature perturbations and linear probing of synthetic network contexts. (Sections 3, 4.1, 4.5 and 4.6)
details.Metrics: Intrinsic metrics include mean pairwise cosine similarity, Mean Cosine Contribution and Centered Kernel Alignment with CICFlowMeter features. Additional analyses report F1 and F1 gain, intrinsic dimension, silhouette score and L1 distance. (Sections 3.1–3.3 and 4.3; Appendices F–H)
details.Reported results: The authors' decorrelation intervention improves NetMamba F1 by 0.35 ± 0.02 on Crossmarket, 0.11 ± 0.27 on CIC-IDS2017 and 0.03 ± 0.02 on CIC-APT-IIoT24. These gains use a single linear layer trained for 30 epochs over five runs. (Section 4.3; Table 2)
details.Reproducibility: No experiments independently rerun for this explorer.
details.Leakage / shortcut risks: The authors identify dataset-specific shortcuts as a weakness of downstream-only evaluation. Their perturbation tests expose payload dependence and selective sensitivity to sequence/acknowledgement numbers, while their limitations acknowledge potentially flawed or biased public datasets. (Sections 2.3, 4.5 and 5)
details.Deployment limitations: The evaluated models depend on payload information that may be encrypted or absent in production, creating a robustness concern. Metric alignment is also weaker on real-world traffic than on controlled datasets. (Sections 4.4 and 4.5)
details.Version notes: NeurIPS 2025 Datasets and Benchmarks Track confirmed by official proceedings, DOI 10.52202/085713-4769. Technical extraction based on arXiv v3, November 2025; source versions are distinguished.
details.Hardware: All experiments run on a single node with 4 A100 GPUs, each with 80 GB GPU RAM, and 512 GB host RAM. (Appendix I)
details.Measurement scope: Use only the setup stated in the cited results; unextracted conditions remain NA.

title: When Simple Model Just Works: Is Network Traffic Classification in Crisis?
summary: Tests a simple nearest-neighbour baseline on 12 datasets and 15 tasks.
contribution: Highlights redundant packet-metadata sequences and split contamination.
limitation: Redundancy findings apply to the examined representations and datasets.
gap: Deduplicate before splitting and retain conflicting-label diagnostics.

details.Research problem: Tests a simple nearest-neighbour baseline on 12 datasets and 15 tasks.
details.Traffic unit definition: Flow-level: each sample is a network flow represented by the packet sizes, inter-packet times and directions of its first N (up to 30) payload packets. (Section 3.1)
details.Input representation: Raw packet-sequence metadata vector (sizes, IPTs in milliseconds, directions as ±1) compared with L1 distance, reweighted by per-dataset factors DIRscale and IPTscale with IPTs clipped at IPTmaxclip. (Section 3.1)
details.Packets / bytes: Only the first N payload packets per flow are used, no payload or header bytes; default N=10 from prior work, Optuna-tuned per dataset to values 5 to 27 in Table 2. (Section 3.1; Table 2)
details.Preprocessing / anonymisation: Datasets taken as curated pre-split tcbench versions; PCAPs converted to flow packet sequences with ipfixprobe; flows shorter than 10 packets filtered for MIRAGE19/22 and UTMOBILENET21, and empty flows and broadcasts filtered for CIC-IDS-2017; no IP or port masking described. (Sections 3.2-3.3)
details.Architecture: Non-parametric k-NN with L1 distance implemented as a Faiss index; prediction is the label of the top-1 nearest training sample, optionally replaced by distance-based majority voting among all training samples within a threshold Tmaj. (Sections 3.2, 3.5)
details.Pretraining objective: NA — no pretraining stage recorded for this contribution
details.Pretraining datasets: NA — no pretraining stage recorded for this contribution
details.Training / evaluation datasets: 12 datasets and 15 tasks (Table 1): CESNET-TLS22 (TLS, 191 classes), CESNET-QUIC22 (QUIC, 102), ISCXVPN2016 (VPN, 2 classes, three label tasks), MIRAGE19 (Android apps, 20), MIRAGE22 (video-meeting apps, 9), UTMOBILENET21 (mobile apps, 17), UCDAVIS19 (QUIC, 5 classes, Script and Human test sets), AppClassNet (TLS, 500 apps), EdgeIIoTset (IIoT, 15), UNSW-NB15 (attacks, 10), CIC-IDS-2017 (attacks, 8), CIC-DoHBrw-2020 (DoH, 2). (Abstract; Section 3.3; Table 1)
details.Split strategy: Flow-level splits per Table 1: CESNET-TLS22/QUIC22 time-based (1M/0.1M/1M), MIRAGE19/22 and UTMOBILENET21 prepared random 80/10/10, ISCXVPN2016 random 60/20/20, UCDAVIS19 fixed (7k train, 83 or 150 test), AppClassNet and EdgeIIoTset random 1M/0.1M/1M, UNSW-NB15, CIC-IDS-2017 and CIC-DoHBrw random 0.5M/0.1M/0.5M; results averaged over five repetitions (one for UCDAVIS19). (Section 3.3; Table 1)
details.Evaluation setting: Evaluation and critique study: the input-space k-NN baseline (default N=10, Optuna-tuned, and with distance-based majority voting) is tested on 12 datasets and 15 tasks against published SOTA numbers under replicated preprocessing and splitting; ISCXVPN2016 is also compared against payload-free SOTA in Table 4. (Section 3.6; Table 4)
details.Metrics: Accuracy is the primary metric, with F1 for three comparisons (MIRAGE19, MIRAGE22, UTMOBILENET21); the paper also defines maximum achievable accuracy (Eq. 1) and a minimal false positive rate estimate; no macro, weighted or micro averaging is stated. (Sections 3.6, 4.2)
details.Reported results: Authors report >50% redundant sequences in most examined datasets; this is not a universal rate.
details.Reproducibility: No experiments independently rerun for this explorer.
details.Leakage / shortcut risks: Authors report and test that most datasets contain over 50% exact duplicate packet sequences which random splits place in both training and test sets, trivially inflating accuracy for distance-based classifiers; duplicate fraction correlates with baseline performance, and on CESNET-QUIC22 the random split gives 79.41 versus 75.53 under a time-based split. Mixed-class duplicates cap maximum achievable accuracy, e.g. 93.46% on UTMOBILENET21. (Abstract; Sections 4.1-4.2, 5.1.2; Tables 5, 8)
details.Deployment limitations: The L1 metric cannot capture differences across packet positions such as missed and retransmitted packets or shifted patterns in the sequence, so the baseline misses such variations. (Section 3.1)
details.Version notes: Table 3 reports F1 for MIRAGE19/MIRAGE22/UTMOBILENET21 while Table 5 recomputes accuracy for these without short-flow filtering (MIRAGE19 80.78 in Table 3 versus 78.56 in Table 5); UCDAVIS19 has no validation set, so it gets no Optuna tuning or majority voting and a single repetition; ISCXVPN2016 uses the preprocessed version of Nascita et al. (10.5k samples), not the original. (Table 5 footnote; Sections 3.3-3.4; Tables 1, 3, 5)
details.Measurement scope: Use only the setup stated in the cited results; unextracted conditions remain NA.

title: One task to rule them all: A closer look at traffic classification generalizability
summary: Evaluates service prediction when training and testing networks differ.
contribution: Separates real-world distribution shift from concept drift in two TLS collections.
limitation: This evaluation is a particular service-prediction task, not all traffic classification.
gap: Robust cross-organisation service inference with hidden SNI.

details.Research problem: Evaluates service prediction when training and testing networks differ.
details.Traffic unit definition: The principal transfer task classifies bidirectional flows, allowing source and destination endpoint pairs to be reversed. Earlier comparisons separately classify website traces and fixed-duration unidirectional flow snapshots. (Sections 4.1.1 and 5; Appendices C.1–C.3)
details.Input representation: The aligned transfer input contains inter-arrival times, payload sizes and packet directions, with MinMax normalisation used by default. (Section 5.2.5)
details.Packets / bytes: Aligned inputs contain the first 30 non-empty packets of each bidirectional flow, giving a shared input shape of (30,3). (Sections 5.2.5 and 5.3)
details.Preprocessing / anonymisation: Orange is relabelled using CESNET's SNI mapping, common frequent classes are selected and CESNET is undersampled into balanced splits. Inter-arrival times are capped at 5 seconds, negative CESNET values become zero and Orange inputs are reconstructed to match CESNET's payload-bearing packets. (Sections 5.2.3–5.2.5)
details.Architecture: The study designs First Model, More Blocks, New Run and NoMB variants from UWTransformer, also called Full Model. Architectures combine channel-wise multi-head attention, convolutional layers, residual connections and dense classification layers. (Section 5.3; Table 7; Appendices F and H)
details.Pretraining objective: NA — no pretraining stage recorded for this contribution
details.Pretraining datasets: NA — no pretraining stage recorded for this contribution
details.Training / evaluation datasets: Earlier comparisons use Undefended with 95 website classes, ISCX-Flowpic Tor with 5 application categories and Orange June with 8 service categories. The aligned transfer framework uses 25 common service classes from CESNET and Orange June/October, with 1.2 million, 69.1K and 83.6K selected flows, respectively. (Sections 4.1 and 5.2; Tables 2 and 6)
details.Split strategy: CESNET training/validation and test data come from the first and last three collection days, respectively, with a 4:1 training/validation ratio. For transfer evaluation, models train on CESNET and are tested on the entire aligned Orange selection; snapshot experiments keep origin flows separate across training and test. (Sections 5.2.3 and 6.2; Section 4.2.1; Appendix D)
details.Evaluation setting: DFattack, Flowpic and UWTransformer are first retrained and compared across alternative datasets, separating snapshot classification from flow/trace classification. The aligned service-identification framework then compares transformer variants, XGBoost and cosine-distance 1-NN through same-dataset and cross-network evaluation, including reverse transfer and grouped-label tasks. (Sections 4, 5 and 6; Tables 1, 7–9)
details.Metrics: The study reports accuracy, precision, recall and F1-score. Snapshot comparisons explicitly use the unweighted average of classwise F1-scores. (Section 4.2.3; Figures 5–7; Tables 8 and 9)
details.Reported results: Best model under the network shift: the Full Model, the paper’s alias for UWTransformer (a transformer classifier on flow time series from Critical Study of Few-shot Learning for Encrypted Traffic Classification, CNSM 2023). F1 0.3174 (accuracy 0.3015) on Orange June and F1 0.3063 (0.2767) on Orange October, against F1 0.9274 on the CESNET test set. 1-NN and XGBoost also fall to F1 0.25–0.26.
details.Parameters: Total parameter counts are 60,439 for First Model, 62,001 for MoreBlocks, 12,117 for NewRun, 121,801 for NoMB and 8,222,873 for Full Model. (Appendix H; Tables 10, 12, 14, 15 and 16)
details.Latency: UWTransformer's average training computation time is 18 milliseconds per batch of 64 samples, compared with 5 milliseconds for DFattack on the authors' GPU. (Appendix F)
details.Reproducibility: No experiments independently rerun for this explorer.
details.Leakage / shortcut risks: The authors identify dataset-specific characteristics, selection cutoffs and hyperparameter choices as causes of inflated same-dataset performance. They prevent snapshots from the same flow crossing training/test boundaries, but explicitly derive snapshot validation data without respecting origin flows. (Sections 4.2.1, 4.4 and 7; Appendix D)
details.Deployment limitations: Distribution shift substantially degrades classification even without concept drift, and task-related knowledge is insufficient for reliable use. Best performance also depends on training choices and hyperparameters that may be unavailable under realistic conditions. (Sections 4.4 and 7)
details.Version notes: NA — not extracted
details.Hardware: GPU computation is reported, without a GPU model specification. (Appendix F)
details.Measurement scope: The reported computation time measures GPU training of a batch; no live classification pipeline timing is provided. (Appendix F)

title: FlowletFormer: Network Behavioral Semantic Aware Pre-training Model for Traffic Classification
summary: Segments traffic into behaviour-aware units and aligns protocol-stack embeddings.
contribution: Adds field-specific and contextual pretraining tasks.
limitation: Better semantic probes need independent transfer and deployment validation.
gap: Balance protocol knowledge with efficient processing.

details.Research problem: Segments traffic into behaviour-aware units and aligns protocol-stack embeddings.
details.Traffic unit definition: Five-tuple flow segmented into flowlets where the inter-arrival time exceeds an adaptive threshold, the mean of the IATs in a history window.

title: NetAgent: Multi-Task Agentic Network Traffic Analysis Made Practical
summary: Proposes an agentic framework that handles many traffic analysis tasks, from intrusion detection to encrypted traffic classification, without task-specific training.
contribution: An agent loop plans and decomposes tasks using attack knowledge, 150+ tools extracted from 50+ published systems, a code execution space, three-tier memory and sandboxed runtime repair. title: SCSM: A Traffic-Native Foundation Model for Transferable Website Fingerprinting
summary: Pretrains a traffic-native foundation model for website fingerprinting that transfers across website sets, time, paths, browsers and defences.
contribution: Pretraining views are built from unlabelled traces by Segmentation, Combination, Scaling and Masking; windowed traffic counting matrices train a state-space encoder contrastively, then a small labelled support set fine-tunes it. Reports +16.4% average top-3 accuracy over six temporal-drift tasks on GTT23 and +13.8% average macro-F1 over four cross-domain datasets.

details.Research problem: NA — not extracted
details.Traffic unit definition: Encrypted packet traces containing timestamped packet directions, divided into N non-overlapping windows of length w sampled from 5 to 50 ms, with N equal to 2700 for single-tab tasks and 7200 for multi-tab tasks. (Section IV-B; Section V-A.2)
details.Input representation: Direction-only Windowed Traffic Counting Matrix (WTCM) transformed element-wise by log(1 + M), forming a 4 by N matrix recording outgoing counts, incoming counts, inter-window gap, and packet cluster count. (Section IV-B; Algorithm 1)
details.Architecture: A 4 by 1 convolution projecting each window to embedding dimension 512, followed by four causal convolutional blocks with temporal max pooling (kernel size 5, dropout 0.1), sinusoidal positional embeddings, three Mamba2 blocks with maximum drop-path rate 0.2, temporal mean pooling, and a linear head. (Section IV-D.1; Section V-A.2)
details.Pretraining objective: Symmetric cross-view contrastive loss over views built by Segmentation, Combination, Scaling and Masking. (Section IV-D)
details.Fine-tuning objective: Cross-entropy loss jointly fine-tuning the pretrained encoder and a task-specific linear classification head on a small labeled support set. (Section III-B)
details.Pretraining datasets: First 7 weeks of GTT23, or scenario D1 of Swallow (two separate pretraining sources). (Section V-A)
details.Training / evaluation datasets: Pretrained on GTT23 (weeks 1 to 7) or Swallow D1 (100 websites, 100 traces each); evaluated on GTT23 weeks 8 to 13 (200 websites), Swallow D2 to D7, DFSet (95 websites), simulated W-TSet (100 websites), k-NNSet (100 websites), R-PSet (265 websites), Open-World DFSet (40,000 unmonitored traces), ARESSet (2 to 5 tabs, 100 monitored websites), and Defended DFSet. details.Split strategy: GTT23 temporal drift uses 10 labeled traces per website for adaptation and 5 disjoint traces per website for testing; Swallow uses 10 labeled traces per website for adaptation and 90 for testing; single-tab cross-domain uses 10-shot adaptation; Open-World DFSet uses 10 labeled traces per monitored website and 10 unmonitored traces; multi-tab uses 3,000 labeled traces. (Section V-A.1)

title: VFRDAD: An IoT Encrypted traffic identification method based on multi-scale local information and enhanced global information fusion
summary: Classifies IoT encrypted traffic from session-level grayscale images by fusing local and global features.
contribution: Multi-scale high-pass filtering captures local patterns; a traffic-domain autoencoder and dilated convolutions build a three-channel image for a Vision Transformer; gated attention fuses both. Evaluated on Darknet-dataset-2020, ISCXVPN2016 and CIC-IoT-2023.
limitation: Image representations of raw sessions can carry capture-specific bytes; the abstract reports gains under the evaluated protocols only.
gap: Which image regions drive the decision once headers are masked.

details.Research problem: NA — not extracted
details.Traffic unit definition: A flow is a sequence of packets sharing an identical five-tuple (source/destination IP, source/destination port, transport protocol), ordered by arrival time; bidirectional sessions are used. (Section 3.1)
details.Input representation: Each bidirectional session is mapped to a fixed 784-byte prefix reshaped into a 28×28 single-channel grayscale image. (Section 3.1; Section 4.1)
details.Packets / bytes: Fixed 784 bytes per session (truncation for longer, zero-padding for shorter); no header/payload distinction stated. (Section 3.1; Section 4.1)
details.Preprocessing / anonymisation: Flow separation by five-tuple, anonymisation by setting source/destination IP addresses to 0 in the byte stream, removal of duplicate and no-payload packet streams, zero-padding/truncation to 784 bytes, conversion to hexadecimal byte stream. (Section 3.1)
details.Architecture: Four modules: (1) Multi-scale local feature extraction via Fourier high-pass filtering (D_r ∈ {5,10,15,20}) followed by a 3-layer CNN; (2) Global feature extraction via a traffic-domain autoencoder (3-layer dilated CNN, dilation rate 2, output channels 2) for RGB channel remapping, then a pre-trained ViT; (3) Gated-attention fusion module with 2-layer MLP computing adaptive weights; (4) Classifier. (Section 3.2; Section 3.3; Section 3.4; Fig. 1)
details.Pretraining objective: Traffic-domain autoencoder pretrained self-supervised with MSE on the traffic images; the ViT starts from a pre-trained backbone. (Sections 3.3.1–3.3.2)
details.Pretraining datasets: NA — no pretraining stage recorded for this contribution
details.Training / evaluation datasets: Darknet-dataset-2020 (8 classes: Browsing, Chat, Email, Audio Streaming, Video Streaming, File Transfer, P2P, VoIP across Freenet, Tor, I2P, ZeroNet); ISCXVPN2016 (6 categories: Chat, Email, File Transfer, Streaming, P2P, VoIP in VPN and NoVPN subsets); CIC-IoT-2023 (7 attack categories: DDoS, DoS, Recon, Web-based, Brute Force, Spoofing, Mirai). (Section 4.1; Tables 1–3)

title: Unknown-Traffic Detection, Calibration and Shortcut Reliance in Distilled Encrypted-Traffic Classifiers over One Year
summary: Tests what a distilled student inherits from its teacher beyond accuracy: unknown-traffic detection, calibration, shortcut reliance and behaviour under a year of drift.
contribution: One 101k-parameter student is distilled from two equally accurate teachers (a five-member ensemble and a wider single model). Ten pre-registered hypotheses are tested on CESNET-TLS-Year22 over 18 test windows across 35 weeks; two are supported, and shortcut reliance follows model size, not distillation.
limitation: Single dataset and one student size; transfer findings depend on the scoring rule (logit-based versus feature-space detectors).
gap: Whether the same inheritance pattern appears for pretrained traffic foundation models compressed for the edge.

details.Research problem: NA — not extracted
details.Traffic unit definition: Flow-level: each TLS flow is one sample, represented by its first 30 packets. (Section III-A (Inputs))
details.Input representation: Three per-packet sequences (inter-packet time, direction, size) over the first 30 packets, plus 12 flow statistics and a 32-bin packet-size histogram (44 tabular features); sequences and statistics are scaled with transforms fitted on each training window only. (Section III-A (Inputs))
details.Packets / bytes: First 30 packets per flow, used only through timing, direction and size; no payload or byte budget is stated. A sensitivity analysis also reports flows with at least five packets (94.0% of test flows). (Section III-A (Inputs); Section IV-A)
details.Preprocessing / anonymisation: Server name, IP addresses, ports, autonomous system and JA3 fingerprint are excluded from the inputs, so the classifier sees what it would see under Encrypted Client Hello; scaling transforms are fitted per training window. Each test flow carries a duplicate flag (64-bit hash of the scaled sequence) and 1.8% of test flows exactly occur in their training window, removed in a sensitivity analysis. (Section III-A (Inputs; Time structure); Section IV-A)
details.Architecture: Student: multimodal 1D-CNN with three convolutions (48, 96, 96 channels; kernels 5, 5, 3) over the packet sequences pooled by mean and max, a 64-unit layer over the flow statistics, a 128-unit shared layer with dropout 0.1 and a linear classifier. Teacher A is a five-member ensemble of mm_cesnet_v2 multimodal CNNs (mean of member softmax outputs); Teacher B is a single wider network of the same family (three convolutional blocks of 400/600/600 channels, two 450-unit statistics layers, a 1,200-unit shared layer); an exploratory Teacher C is a transformer encoder over the packet sequence. (Section III-B (Models); Section V-B)
details.Pretraining objective: NA — no pretraining stage recorded for this contribution
details.Fine-tuning objective: There is no pretraining or fine-tuning; students are trained from scratch. Hinton KD minimises αT²KL(teacher‖student) + (1−α)CE with α = 0.9 at T ∈ {1, 4}; controls are direct cross-entropy, post-hoc temperature scaling, label smoothing ε = 0.05 and proxy-Dirichlet EnDD with reverse-KL (precision capped at 10⁴). All networks use AdamW (learning rate 10⁻³, weight decay 10⁻⁴), a one-cycle schedule with 10% warm-up, batch size 1,024 and bf16 autocast; teachers 10 epochs, students 20. (Section III-C (Training Conditions); Table I)
details.Pretraining datasets: NA — no pretraining stage recorded for this contribution
details.Training / evaluation datasets: CESNET-TLS-Year22 only: the S subset (25M flows) of one year (2022) of TLS flows from the Czech national research network, accessed via cesnet-datazoo 0.2.0, with 180 services labelled from the server name. 102 services are known classes; held-out unknowns differ between validation (far: Music and Videoconferencing, 8 services, plus 5 near) and test (far: Search and Social, 11 services, plus 8 near), and 46 further services are excluded, mostly for insufficient or inconsistent volume. (Section III-A (Dataset; Known and unknown services))
details.Split strategy: Time-ordered, three replicates by training start date: training on weeks 11-14, 24-27 and 37-40 (1.89M, 1.37M and 1.35M known flows), validation on the following week (200k known flows plus all validation-unknown flows), then consecutive 4-week test windows to week 52, giving 9, 6 and 3 windows (18 total), each a stratified sample of 100k known and 100k unknown flows at 3.5 to 35.3 weeks after training. The service split (102 known, seed 2022) was generated once before any model was trained. (Section III-A (Time structure; Known and unknown services))
details.Metrics: Closed-set macro-F1 (macro averaging stated); unknown-detection AUROC and FPR at 95% TPR under two unknown-scores, the energy score (log-sum-exp of the logits) and maximum softmax probability (MSP), with known flows as positives; OSCR; ECE (15 bins), NLL and Brier score before and after temperature scaling; AURC; and Spearman correlation of per-flow energy scores for inheritance. (Section III-D (Outcomes))
details.Reported results: Averaged over the 18 test windows (Table II): direct student 0.806 macro-F1 and 0.835 energy AUROC; kdA (T=1) 0.806 and 0.834 (indistinguishable from direct and directTS); kdA4 (T=4) 0.790 and 0.809; ls 0.797 and 0.814; enddA 0.801 and 0.742 (worst energy detector); Teacher A 0.860 and 0.836. Teachers are 4.8 to 7.1 macro-F1 points more accurate but only 0.001 energy AUROC better at detection; H1 is supported (kdA4 +0.007, kdB4 +0.026 own-teacher shift, Holm p = 0.009) and H3 reversed (teacher-student energy AUROC slope of -0.0004 per week); under feature-space scores Teacher A is 0.073 Mahalanobis AUROC above direct, kdA4 recovers +0.076, and label smoothing beats kdA4 by +0.011. (Table II; Table III; Section IV; Section V-A)
details.Parameters: Student 101,190 parameters (101k), 22× smaller than one teacher member and 112× smaller than the ensemble; Teacher A members 2.26M each (11.3M as an ensemble), Teacher B 10.3M, exploratory transformer Teacher C 3.5M. (Section III-B; Section V-B; Table II)
details.Latency: Student in ONNX Runtime: 0.082 ms p50 and 0.160 ms p99 per flow (batch size 1, one thread); Teacher A ensemble 19.093 ms p50; XGBoost 41.606 ms. Offline forward pass only. (Table VII; Section IV-E)
details.Throughput: Student 21,201 flows/s on one thread (ONNX Runtime); PyTorch student 39,418 flows/s on all cores; Teacher A 161 flows/s. (Table VII)
details.Memory: Serialised weights: student 0.4 MB, Teacher A 45.4 MB, Teacher B 41.3 MB, XGBoost 244.4 MB. (Table VII)
details.Reproducibility: NA — not extracted
details.Deployment limitations: Stated: novelty is simulated (no service first appears mid-year), the study is one dataset, one network, one year, and the confirmatory grid uses a single teacher architecture at two widths, with the transformer teacher exploratory on one start date. Also stated: natural shortcut fields (server IP, ASN, JA3) were excluded from the inputs, not tested; the shortcut experiment plants a synthetic feature on the validation week at a single student width; H1's support rests more on kdB4 than kdA4 (kdA4 null at start date 11 unexplained); baselines and deployment cost were measured on the validation week and a laptop CPU; deposited per-flow score files store MSP in float16, which saturates confident flows; the feature-distillation arm carries an untuned loss weight (β = 100). (Section VI (Limitations); Section V-G; Section VII)
details.Version notes: Preprint, September 2026 (arXiv:2609.31141v1, 25 Sep 2026), pre-registered at OSF and frozen at repository commit fa8f718 after a pilot and validation-only design phase, with all Section V analyses added after the confirmatory results were known. Timing numbers come from two sessions: the text quotes the student at 0.08 ms while Table VII gives 0.082 ms p50, and the re-tuned XGBoost comparison uses its own session (14.4 ms against 0.072 ms for the student). (Front page and footer; Section III; Section IV-E; Table VII)
details.Hardware: Inference was measured on a laptop CPU (AMD Ryzen 7 5800H, 8 cores) as a stand-in for an edge device; no training or GPU hardware is stated. (Section IV-E; Table VII)
details.Measurement scope: The efficiency numbers cover offline model forward-pass inference only: per-flow latency at batch size 1 on one thread, throughput at batch size 1,024, and serialised model size; they do not cover feature extraction, capture or a live pipeline. The teachers could not be exported to ONNX Runtime, so only the student was timed in ONNX, and the re-tuned XGBoost was timed in a separate session. (Table VII caption; Section IV-E)

title: Shortcut in Generalization: Rethinking Evaluation Protocol for Encrypted Traffic Classification
summary: Studies how evaluation protocols inflate encrypted traffic classification results through field-level shortcuts, cross-partition sharing and test-only transformations.
contribution: Compares feature importance, retrained feature removal and field-only split sensitivity on three public datasets, varying Source-IP overlap and packets per flow. Raising Source-IP overlap from 0% to 100% adds about 32–33 accuracy points before identifier masking and about 8 after; for YaTC and NetMamba the 11–13 point loss from test-only IP zeroing is almost fully recovered when the same transformation is applied in training.
limitation: The three datasets are not named in the abstract; results cover the methods the authors retrained.
gap: An evaluation protocol that fixes sharing and train–test processing before any model comparison.

details.Research problem: NA — not extracted
details.Traffic unit definition: Packet experiments use individual packets; flow experiments construct samples from packets belonging to the same bidirectional parent flow. (Section III-A; Table I)
details.Input representation: The field-text view uses field–value tokens encoded as 10,000-dimensional TF-IDF features with 1–3-grams and a LinearSVC classifier. Byte-based experiments use model-specific packet or flow representations. (Sections III-A and IV-A(a); Table I)
details.Packets / bytes: The principal flow inputs contain the first five packets of each parent flow. (Section III-A; Table I)
details.Preprocessing / anonymisation: Cumulative masking removes MAC addresses and frame.number, then IP addresses including IPv6, then transport ports, with independent retraining for each condition. Separate byte transformations compare original addresses, per-flow IP remapping and IP zeroing under test-only and matched training–test processing. (Sections III-B and III-D)

title: NetLexicon: Learning Discrete Behavioral Representations for Encrypted Web Traffic Analysis
summary: Pretrains discrete behavioural states from unlabelled encrypted Web traffic as a compact traffic lexicon.
contribution: Vector quantisation turns contextual traffic windows into discrete states, trained with State Transition Prediction and Statistical Feature Alignment. On four benchmarks (Web application, service type, malware) it reports up to 25.5 points higher macro-F1 than the strongest baseline and up to 23.6× less fine-tuning time per epoch.
limitation: Benchmarks are not named in the abstract; interpretability is shown by inspecting learned states.
gap: Whether a learned traffic lexicon stays stable across capture sites and years.

details.Research problem: NA — not extracted
details.Traffic unit definition: Bidirectional flow defined by 5-tuple, ordered chronologically, parsed into bursts of consecutive same-direction packets and sliding windows of 5 consecutive bursts. (Section 3.1)
details.Input representation: Sequences of packet tokens with inserted [SEP] after each burst and [WIN] after every W bursts. Each packet token consists of 7 normalized features concatenated with 7 binary missing indicators to form a 14-dimensional vector, alongside separate embeddings for token types and positions. (Section 3.1; Appendix A)
details.Packets / bytes: Maximum sequence length of 256 tokens. Sliding windows contain 5 consecutive bursts. (Section 3.1; Section 4.1)
details.Preprocessing / anonymisation: SplitCap is used to extract bidirectional flows. Flows containing fewer than one complete window of 5 consecutive bursts are discarded. Explicit avoidance of raw IP addresses, port numbers, TTL, and raw IPID. (Table 2; Section 4.1)
details.Architecture: Four-layer causal transformer encoder with hidden size 192, feed-forward size 768, 16 attention heads, followed by a VQ-VAE discrete lexicon layer with a codebook of 128 codewords, and two projection heads for SFA. (Section 3.2; Section 4.1)
details.Pretraining objective: State Transition Prediction (token type prediction and packet feature regression), codebook commitment with EMA updates, and Statistical Feature Alignment (InfoNCE over 37 window statistics). (Section 3.5)
details.Fine-tuning objective: Cross-entropy loss on labeled flows using a pooled [WIN] representation passed through a task-specific classification head, trained in two stages (frozen backbone first, then joint end-to-end). (Section 3.5; Section 4.1)
details.Pretraining datasets: 1,057,331 flows (about 86.34 million packets) from MAWI and VisQUIC. (Section 4.1)
details.Training / evaluation datasets: CSTNET (Web APP fingerprinting, 120 classes, 45.16K flows), CipherSpectrum (Web APP fingerprinting, 42 classes, 164.2K flows), ISCXVPN (Service type identification, 7 classes, 2.184K flows), and USTC-TFC (Malware detection, 17 classes, 114.3K flows). (Table 3)
details.Split strategy: Flow-level random split within each class using an 8:1:1 train:validation:test ratio with seed 42; all windows from the same flow remain in the same partition. (Section 4.1)
details.Metrics: Accuracy, macro-precision, macro-recall, and Macro-F1. (Section 4.1)
details.Reported results: ISCXVPN: 0.8267 accuracy, 0.8034 Macro-F1; USTC-TFC: 0.9889 accuracy, 0.9547 Macro-F1; CSTNET: 0.8838 accuracy, 0.8637 Macro-F1; CipherSpectrum: 0.9104 accuracy, 0.9002 Macro-F1. (Tables 4 and 5)
details.Latency: 11.1 ms offline batch inference latency at batch size 32; fine-tuning 3.0 minutes per epoch. (Section 4.4)
details.Memory: 0.9 GB GPU memory at batch size 32. (Section 4.4)
details.Reproducibility: NA — not extracted
details.Deployment limitations: Performance relies on recurring observable behavior consistency, which changes across varying network conditions or protocol implementations, requiring adaptation of encoder and codebook; producing contextual window representations still requires neural computation. (Section 5)
details.Version notes: NA — not extracted
details.Measurement scope: Measurements reflect GPU neural computation for model fine-tuning and batch inference, but exclude full encoding pipeline costs such as state assignment generation. (Section 5)
