title: Curv-Tail: Lightweight Long-Tailed Encrypted Traffic Classification with Discrete Packet-Length Encoding and Lorentz Prototypes
summary: Targets long-tailed encrypted traffic classification under a small compute budget, without a separate pretraining stage.
contribution: Mixed-resolution tokens keep exact packet lengths within a bounded range; an auxiliary task predicts length tokens; compact temporal encoders read packet sequences and directional byte patches, classified by Lorentz prototypes. Three-seed mean Tail-F1 is 85.70% on NUDT-Mobile and 46.30% on DataCon-Website; on an RTX 4090 it uses 98.48% fewer parameters and 10.2× the batch inference throughput of MM4Flow.
limitation: Throughput is offline batch inference (FP32, batch 256), not a live rate.
gap: How tail-class accuracy holds when the head classes drift over time.

details.Research problem: NA — not extracted
details.Traffic unit definition: Samples are bidirectional flows grouped by five-tuple; the model uses up to 64 packets per flow. (Section 3.1, Datasets and baselines; Implementation)
details.Input representation: The packet view combines mixed-resolution discrete length tokens with direction, log-transformed inter-arrival time and position embeddings. The byte view embeds upstream and downstream bytes separately and compresses them into non-overlapping patches using a strided convolution. (Section 2.1, Equation (1))
details.Packets / bytes: Inputs contain up to 64 packets per flow and 256 bytes per direction. (Section 3.1, Implementation)
details.Preprocessing / anonymisation: After bidirectional five-tuple grouping, flows with fewer than five packets are removed. Length tokenisation preserves exact identities within a bounded range and coarsens larger lengths. (Sections 3.1 and 2.1)
details.Architecture: Separate packet and byte encoders use gated residual dilated convolutions with Lorentz logarithmic and exponential maps; packet features use learned-query attention pooling and byte features use masked mean pooling. Their projected concatenation is classified by trainable Lorentz prototypes with shared learnable curvature, alongside an auxiliary packet-length retention head. (Sections 2.2 and 2.3, Equations (2)–(3); Figure 2)
details.Pretraining objective: NA — no pretraining stage recorded for this contribution
details.Fine-tuning objective: Training from scratch jointly minimises flow-level cross-entropy and auxiliary cross-entropy predicting observed length tokens from packet features before pooling. The retention task uses unmasked, uncorrupted tokens and does not modify class priors or prediction logits. (Sections 2.2 and 2.3, Equation (3); Section 3.1)
details.Pretraining datasets: NA — no pretraining stage recorded for this contribution
details.Training / evaluation datasets: DataCon-Website contains 100 website classes over encrypted tunnels and 85,146 retained flows; NUDT-Mobile contains 300 mobile-app classes and 1,282,557 retained flows. Both retain naturally long-tailed class frequencies. (Section 3.1, Datasets and baselines; Table 1)
details.Split strategy: All methods share a fixed, class-stratified 7:1:2 training/validation/test split at flow level for closed-set classification; checkpoints are selected using validation Macro-F1. (Section 3.1, Datasets and baselines; Implementation)
details.Metrics: ACC and Macro-F1 cover all classes; Tail-F1 averages per-class F1 over tail classes, while Tail-R measures the fraction of correctly classified test flows whose true labels are tail classes. Classes ranked by decreasing training frequency form head/body/tail groups containing 50%/30%/20% of classes, and main results average seeds 42, 2027 and 3407. (Section 3.1, Metrics and runs; Table 1 caption)
details.Reported results: On NUDT-Mobile, three-seed mean ACC, Macro-F1 and Tail-F1 are 96.70%, 93.48% and 85.70%; on DataCon-Website they are 73.53%, 66.66% and 46.30%, respectively. (Table 1, Curv-Tail row; Section 3.2)
details.Parameters: The default model has 0.84M parameters for 300 classes and 0.82M for 100 classes, with the difference confined to the classification head. (Figure 4 caption)
details.Latency: Amortised batch forward time 0.1359 ms per flow (median batch time divided by batch size), offline. (Section 3.4)
details.Throughput: 10.2× MM4Flow’s batch inference throughput in 300-class profiling (RTX 4090, FP32, batch 256). (Section 3.4)
details.Reproducibility: NA — not extracted
details.Deployment limitations: NA — not extracted
details.Version notes: Reviewed arXiv v2 (10 October 2026). The third and seventh authors, both named Lin Liu, are different people (paper footnote).
details.Hardware: Efficiency profiling uses an RTX 4090 with FP32 and batch size 256. (Section 3.4; Abstract)
details.Measurement scope: Efficiency profiling measures amortised model forward time and retains the auxiliary retention head; counted MACs exclude element-wise operations. (Section 3.4)

title: PMP-Net: A packet-level multi-branch prototype network for few-shot and open-set encrypted traffic classification
summary: Classifies individual encrypted packets in few-shot and open-set settings.
contribution: Separate branches read packet headers and payloads, joined by bidirectional multi-head attention; prototypes with a similarity-threshold rejection flag unknown classes. Reports 98.9% and 99.2% accuracy on ISCX and USTC-TFC2016 with millisecond-level inference latency.
limitation: Packet-level header input can expose identifiers; the abstract does not say which ISCX collection is used.
gap: Whether the rejection threshold holds for unknown classes from a different capture.

details.Research problem: NA — not extracted
details.Traffic unit definition: Packet-level: individual packets serve as the classification units, with each captured flow segmented into single packets during preprocessing. (Sections 3.2 and 4.1)
details.Input representation: A packet is decomposed into a fixed-length header byte sequence encoded with byte plus positional embeddings, and a payload represented as a normalised 256-dimensional byte-value histogram; an FFT of the histogram yields a 512-dimensional frequency-domain vector for the payload branch. (Sections 3.2-3.3)
details.Packets / bytes: One packet per sample; the header is standardised to 64 bytes (longer truncated, shorter zero-padded), while the payload is not segmented or truncated and all valid payload bytes are counted into the histogram. (Section 3.2)
details.Preprocessing / anonymisation: Duplicate and empty packets are removed, IP and MAC addresses are erased for anonymisation, and control packets carrying only SYN, ACK or FIN flags without payload are discarded; header lengths are then standardised by cropping or zero-padding. (Section 3.2)
details.Architecture: Dual-branch design: header branch with multi-scale depthwise-separable 1D convolutions (kernels 3 and 5), a residual block with SE attention, a GLU, a two-layer Transformer encoder and global average pooling to a 128-d header vector; payload branch with FFT over the histogram and a two-layer MLP to 128 dimensions; bidirectional multi-head attention fusion, then a prototype classifier with cosine margin and similarity-threshold unknown rejection. (Sections 3.3-3.5)
details.Pretraining objective: NA — no pretraining stage recorded for this contribution
details.Fine-tuning objective: Episodic 5-way-10-shot training minimises cross-entropy loss with label smoothing (0.1) over margin-penalised, temperature-scaled cosine similarities to class prototypes, using Adam with warmup and cosine-annealing scheduling and early stopping. (Sections 3.5 and 4.4)
details.Pretraining datasets: NA — no pretraining stage recorded for this contribution
details.Training / evaluation datasets: ISCX VPN-nonVPN (14 classes, 79,315 samples, 16.3 GB) and USTC-TFC2016 (10 classes, 172,048 samples, 3.2 GB); open-set experiments designate a subset of categories as unknown, excluded from training and used only at test time. (Section 4.1; Table 1)
details.Split strategy: Random packet-level split into training, validation and test sets at 8:1:1; open-set classes are wholly excluded from training and introduced only at test time. (Section 4.1)
details.Metrics: Accuracy, precision, recall and F1-score for closed-set classification; TPR, FPR and AUROC for open-set rejection; no averaging scheme (macro or weighted) is stated. (Section 4.2)
details.Reported results: Accuracy 98.9% on ISCX VPN-nonVPN (precision 0.99, recall 0.988, F1 0.989) and 99.2% on USTC-TFC2016 (precision 0.996, recall 0.994, F1 0.995). Open-set AUROC peaks at 0.8243 at similarity threshold 0.70. (Abstract; Tables 2–3; Section 4.6)
details.Latency: Average model inference latency 5.75 ms per packet on the authors’ workstation; no throughput or memory figures. (Section 4.8; Table 6)
details.Reproducibility: NA — not extracted
details.Deployment limitations: The authors acknowledge PMP-Net is slightly slower per packet than the lightweight ECM (1.57 ms) and SAM (2.56 ms) baselines, though it is more accurate. (Section 4.8)
details.Version notes: The ablation text reports 99.50% USTC-TFC2016 accuracy for the full model, while the abstract and Table 3 report 99.2%. (Section 4.5; Table 3)
details.Hardware: Windows 11 workstation with a 12th Gen Intel Core i5-12500H processor (12 cores, 16 threads), 32 GB DDR5 4800 MHz RAM and an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3050 Laptop GPU (4 GB VRAM); Python 3.10.13 with PyTorch and CUDA. (Section 4.4)
details.Measurement scope: Efficiency numbers cover per-packet model inference latency only; preprocessing cost, memory usage and end-to-end pipeline throughput are not reported. (Section 4.8; Table 6)

title: DPFT: A dual-phase transformer with pre-training and structurally adaptive fine-tuning for encrypted traffic classification
summary: Couples traffic-oriented pretraining with a fine-tuning structure designed for downstream classification.
contribution: Pretraining combines Masked Burst Prediction and Burst Structural Discrimination; fine-tuning adds dynamic embedding fusion and multi-head attention pooling. Within-dataset closed-set macro-F1: CSTNET-TLS 1.3 93.10%, ISCX-VPN-App 97.92%, ISCX-VPN-Service 95.65%, USTC-TFC 2016 98.87%.
limitation: The authors state that robustness to temporal or cross-domain shift, unseen classes and deployment conditions remains unverified.
gap: Whether burst-structure pretraining helps under a capture-disjoint split.

details.Research problem: NA — not extracted
details.Traffic unit definition: The unit is the bidirectional session (packets in temporal order, five-tuple used only for reconstruction); sessions are partitioned into direction-continuous bursts for pre-training, and each fine-tuning sample takes the session's first 10 packets. (Section 3.1; Eqs. (2)-(3); Table 2)
details.Input representation: Sanitized Byte-Bigram tokens generated within each packet, with a [PKT] boundary token between adjacent packets; [CLS] is prepended and sequences are padded or truncated to a maximum encoder length of 648 tokens. (Section 3.1; Algorithm 1; Table 2)
details.Packets / bytes: First 10 packets per session (K=10) with at most 64 retained sanitized bytes per packet (M=64), giving a maximum encoder input of 648 tokens. (Section 3.1; Algorithm 1; Table 2)
details.Preprocessing / anonymisation: PCAPs are standardised with editcap and segmented into bidirectional sessions with SplitCap; link-layer addresses, IP addresses, ports and plaintext host or domain fields are replaced with zero-valued bytes, affected checksums are normalised, and identifiers are not given to the model. (Section 3.1)
details.Architecture: A 12-layer Transformer encoder with hidden size 768, 12 self-attention heads and feedforward size 3072 is shared between pre-training and fine-tuning; fine-tuning adds a Dynamic Weighting module for token and positional embedding fusion, a Mask-aware Multi-Head Attention Pooling module, then a ReLU plus fully connected classifier. (Section 4; Table 2; Sections 3.3.1-3.3.3)
details.Pretraining objective: Masked Burst Prediction (contiguous span masking covering about 20% of retained content tokens; affected tokens masked with 80% probability, replaced by a random token with 10% and kept unchanged with 10%) and Burst Structural Discrimination (binary cross-entropy on adjacent burst pairs versus inter-session, non-adjacent and reversed-order negatives) are jointly optimised with equal weight (λ_BSD = 1). (Section 3.2)
details.Fine-tuning objective: Supervised multi-class cross-entropy over traffic categories; the transferred encoder, DW, MHAP and MLP classification head are jointly optimised for 30 epochs with AdamW (fine-tuning learning rate 2×10^-5, batch size 32). (Section 3.3.3; Table 2)
details.Pretraining datasets: About 30 GB of unlabeled traffic: 15 GB of real-world CSTNET traffic plus approximately 15 GB from the benchmark datasets (ISCX-VPN-App, ISCX-VPN-Service, USTC-TFC 2016); only training-partition sessions are used, over 500,000 steps with checkpoints every 10,000 (AdamW, learning rate 5×10^-5). (Section 4.1; Section 4; Section 3.1; Table 2)
details.Training / evaluation datasets: CSTNET-TLS 1.3 (120 classes, 46,372 flows, 581,709 packets), ISCX-VPN-App (17 classes, 2,329 flows, 77,163 packets), ISCX-VPN-Service (12 classes, 3,694 flows, 60,000 packets) and USTC-TFC 2016 (20 classes, 9,853 flows, 97,115 packets). (Section 4.1; Table 4)
details.Split strategy: Session-level partitioning into 80% training, 10% validation and 10% test per dataset (8:1:1); all samples from one session stay in the same subset and validation or test sessions are excluded from pre-training; evaluation is within-dataset and closed-set. (Section 3.1; Table 2; Section 4.6)
details.Metrics: Accuracy plus macro-averaged precision, recall and F1 (Pr_Macro, Rc_Macro, F1_Macro). (Section 4.2)
details.Reported results: Macro-F1 of 93.10% on CSTNET-TLS 1.3, 97.92% on ISCX-VPN-App, 95.65% on ISCX-VPN-Service and 98.87% on USTC-TFC 2016, with accuracies of 93.01%, 97.95%, 95.66% and 98.87% respectively, exceeding eleven baselines under a within-dataset closed-set protocol. (Abstract; Tables 5-6)
details.Parameters: Full DPFT has 135.10M parameters (22.67 GFLOPs per sample); the variant without MHAP has 132.73M and the variant without DW has 134.11M. (Section 4.8; Table 9)
details.Latency: 12.56 ms per sample at batch size 1, offline (30 warm-up, 200 timed iterations). (Section 4.8; Table 9)
details.Throughput: 289.07 samples/s at batch size 32, offline. (Section 4.8; Table 9)
details.Memory: 526.75 MB peak memory at batch size 1. (Section 4.8; Table 9)
details.Reproducibility: NA — not extracted
details.Deployment limitations: Results are limited to within-dataset closed-set benchmarks and do not establish robustness to temporal or cross-domain shifts, unseen classes or deployment conditions; USTC-TFC 2016 results are not evidence of performance on contemporary encrypted traffic; QUIC was not evaluated. (Section 4.9; Abstract; Section 4.6.2)
details.Version notes: Journal Pre-proof (marked-up revised manuscript) for Computer Networks, received 7 June 2026, revised 4 October 2026, accepted 5 October 2026; the version will undergo further copyediting and is not yet the Version of Record. (Cover page)
details.Hardware: Pre-training on four NVIDIA RTX 2080Ti GPUs (11 GB each); downstream fine-tuning on one NVIDIA RTX 4060 GPU (8 GB). (Section 4 (experimental setup))
details.Measurement scope: The efficiency numbers cover offline model inference under the reported hardware and experimental configuration only; system behaviour under operational deployment conditions has not been evaluated. (Section 4.8)

title: NetCoFi: A Budget-Aware Coarse-Fine Dual-Branch Model for Encrypted Traffic Classification
summary: Lets one encrypted traffic classifier trade accuracy for compute at inference time.
contribution: Byte representations and packet metadata select token neighbourhoods for fine-grained encoding while the full window is compressed into coarse context; multi-budget training serves several routing budgets without retraining. Six public datasets; at low budgets +7.86 macro-F1 points over a same-depth static baseline on three; in a DPDK–GPU pipeline mean batch throughput rises from 26.42 to 43.42 Mb/s, 1.64× NetMamba.
limitation: Datasets are not named in the abstract; throughput is mean batch throughput in the authors’ pipeline.
gap: How routing budgets should be set when traffic mix changes during deployment.

details.Research problem: NA — not extracted
details.Traffic unit definition: The main sample is a fixed flow window containing the first packets of a flow. The deployment assembler groups both directions using a canonical bidirectional five-tuple and constructs an input once five packets are available. (Sections III-B and IV-H)
details.Input representation: Concatenated packet header and payload bytes are projected into stride tokens by a one-dimensional convolution. Tokens also receive metadata features describing timing, length, direction, TCP flags, protocol and position. (Section III-B, Equation (1); Table I)
details.Packets / bytes: The default input uses five packets, with each packet's header truncated or padded to 80 bytes and payload truncated or padded to 240 bytes. (Section III-B)
details.Preprocessing / anonymisation: Continuous side features are normalised using training-set statistics, with the same transformation applied to validation and test data. The auxiliary strict-split analysis clears IP addresses and ports, retains flows with at least five packets for flow classification, and balances training and validation classes by undersampling. (Sections III-B and IV-F)
details.Architecture: Learned importance scores select seed-token neighbourhoods for a fine Mamba branch, while anti-importance weighted pooling compresses the full sequence for a separate coarse Mamba branch. A coarse-summary channel gate modulates fine features before pooled branch outputs are concatenated for classification. (Sections III-C and III-D, Equations (2)–(10); Figure 2)
details.Pretraining objective: NA — no pretraining stage recorded for this contribution
details.Fine-tuning objective: Downstream multi-budget training combines supervised classification loss, distillation from the full-budget prediction and a penalty aligning mean importance with the requested seed-token ratio. Each minibatch evaluates endpoint budgets and uniformly sampled intermediate budgets. (Section III-E, Equations (11)–(14); Section IV-A(d))
details.Pretraining datasets: NA — no pretraining stage recorded for this contribution
details.Training / evaluation datasets: The main datasets are CipherSpectrum, CSTNET-TLS1.3, ISCXTOR2016, ISCXVPN2016, USTC-TFC2016 and CTU-13, using balanced subsets for the Tor and VPN datasets and stratified sampling for USTC-TFC2016. Auxiliary strict-split tasks are VPN-app with 16 classes and TLS-120 with 120 classes. (Sections IV-A(a) and IV-F; Tables II, III and VI)
details.Split strategy: The main evaluation uses an 8:1:1 training/validation/test split; CTU-13 additionally keeps captures disjoint while preserving class proportions through proportional sampling. Auxiliary strict-split tasks partition at flow level so constituent packets remain in the same subset, with undersampling confined to training and validation. (Sections IV-A(a) and IV-F)
details.Metrics: Classification metrics are accuracy and Macro-F1; efficiency metrics are inference latency, throughput and peak GPU memory. Model throughput uses samples/s, while deployment pipeline throughput uses Mb/s. (Section IV-A(c))
details.Reported results: Without pretraining, Macro-F1 is 92.81% on ISCXTOR2016, 91.92% on ISCXVPN2016, 97.01% on USTC-TFC2016, 74.79% on CTU-13, 82.75% on CSTNET-TLS1.3 and 45.16% on CipherSpectrum. With pretraining, the corresponding scores are 94.48%, 94.40%, 97.38%, 74.51%, 89.35% and 61.69%. (Tables II and III, NetCoFi rows)
details.Throughput: Mean batch throughput 43.42 Mb/s in the authors’ DPDK–GPU pipeline, against 26.42 Mb/s for NetMamba (1.64×). Model-only latency, throughput and GPU memory are measured separately after warm-up. (Sections IV-C(4), IV-H; Figures 6, 8)
details.Reproducibility: NA — not extracted
details.Deployment limitations: Reducing the routing budget below the useful middle range causes substantial classification degradation. (Section IV-C(1))
details.Version notes: NA — not extracted
details.Hardware: Experiments use NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4090 GPUs with PyTorch 2.8.0 and CUDA 12.8; NetCoFi training uses FP32. (Section IV-A(d))
details.Measurement scope: Deployment batch throughput runs from DPDK-delivered packets to predictions, including flow aggregation, feature construction, routing and GPU inference, while excluding disk I/O and offline trace loading. Separate model inference timings include token selection and routing but exclude data loading. (Sections IV-H and IV-C(4))

details.Research problem: Selects traffic-analysis models online as processing conditions change.
details.Traffic unit definition: Flow-level processing with per-flow state; early detection tasks use first 10 packets per connection. (Section 2.1; Section 3.2; Section 4.2)
details.Input representation: Network flow metrics, transport layer indicators, application-layer traffic pattern features, and raw IP/TCP headers. (Section 4.2)
details.Packets / bytes: Service recognition uses first 10 packets per flow; video quality uses continuous feature extraction; CAIDA trace at 1.1 MPPS. (Section 2.3; Section 4.2; Section 5)
details.Preprocessing / anonymisation: Header parsing, packet filtering, flow tracking, data reassembly; CAIDA Anonymized Internet Traces 2016 used. (Section 2.1; Section 3.2; Section 5)
details.Architecture: Workers for feature extraction, Post-Processor for aggregation, Monitor for packet loss detection, Model Selection module; Rust with DPDK and Retina v0.1. (Section 3; Section 4.1)
details.Pretraining objective: NA — not extracted
details.Pretraining datasets: NA — not extracted
details.Training / evaluation datasets: Bronzino et al. [12] video quality dataset for training; CAIDA Anonymized Internet Traces 2016 (20160121) from Equinix Chicago for evaluation. (Section 4.2; Section 5)
details.Evaluation setting: Compared against Retina and CATO static configurations using TRex-generated CAIDA traffic; single Worker core except for multi-core scalability tests. (Section 5; Section 5.1)
details.Metrics: Median Absolute Error (MAE) in ms for video quality; packet loss percentage; median accuracy. (Table 1; Section 5)
details.Reported results: Cruise Control improves median task accuracy by 2.78% and reduces packet loss by a factor of four versus static models; video quality: 0.37% loss with m3 median accuracy; service recognition: 0.117% vs 0.343% loss for static m3. (Abstract; Section 5.1; Tables 4-5)
details.Throughput: 10 Gbps average with 1.1 MPPS for CAIDA trace; up to 3 Mcps (million connections/second) with 8 workers in worst-case new connection scenario. (Section 5; Table 6)
details.Memory: 384GiB DDR4 per server; thread-local hashmaps can cause memory exhaustion with many workers or long export windows. (Section 5; Section 5.3)
details.Reproducibility: NA — not extracted
details.Deployment limitations: Feature export halts traffic processing for several seconds; thread-local hashmaps risk memory exhaustion; AMD CPUs preclude Intel DDIO; requires careful parameter calibration. (Section 3.2; Section 5; Section 5.3)

details.Measurement scope: Packet loss rates, feature extraction throughput, and model accuracy; covers feature computation and export pipeline but not ML inference. (Section 5; Section 5.1)
details.Hardware: Dual 16-core AMD EPYC 7343 CPUs, 100GbE Intel E810 NIC, 384GiB DDR4 per server; servers connected via 100GbE switch; TRex traffic generator. (Section 5)

title: Data Augmentation for Traffic Classification
summary: Compares augmentation choices for packet time series.
contribution: Benchmarks 18 transformations on three datasets.
limitation: Curator: Benefits are representation- and training-condition-dependent.

details.Research problem: Compares augmentation choices for packet time series.
details.Traffic unit definition: Each sample represents the first 20 packets of a flow, with zero padding at the tail where required. (Section 4.1, Data folds and normalization)
details.Input representation: A multivariate packet time series contains packet size, direction and inter-arrival time. (Section 4.1, Data folds and normalization)
details.Packets / bytes: The input budget is 20 packets per flow. (Section 3.1)
details.Preprocessing / anonymisation: MIRAGE-19 and MIRAGE-22 are curated to remove background traffic and flows with fewer than 10 packets; Enterprise requires no specific preprocessing. Packet sizes and inter-arrival times are clipped, inter-arrival times are logarithmically scaled, and features are normalised. (Section 4.1, Data curation; Data folds and normalization)
details.Architecture: A one-dimensional CNN uses a backbone with two ResNet blocks followed by a linear classification head. (Section 4.1, Model architecture and training; Figure 7)
details.Pretraining objective: NA — not extracted
details.Pretraining datasets: NA — not extracted
details.Training / evaluation datasets: The benchmark uses MIRAGE-19 with 20 classes and 64k curated flows, MIRAGE-22 with nine classes and 26k curated flows, and the private Enterprise dataset with 100 classes and 2.9 million flows. (Section 4.1; Table 4)
details.Split strategy: The curated flow datasets are divided into 80 random train/validation/test splits with proportions 70/15/15; normalisation and augmentation statistics are extracted from the combined training and validation portions. (Section 4.1, Data folds and normalization)
details.Evaluation setting: The CNN benchmark compares 18 augmentation functions from amplitude, masking and sequence families, including individual and combined transformations. It investigates augmentation magnitude, Replace/Inject/Pre-augment batching policies and class-weighted sampling against training without augmentation. (Sections 3.1–3.4, 4.1 and 5.1–5.4)
details.Metrics: Classification is measured with weighted F1, reported as an average across 80 runs with confidence intervals. (Sections 4.1 and 5.1; Table 5)
details.Reported results: Translation improves weighted F1 by 4.40 ± 0.13 points on MIRAGE-19, Wrap by 2.09 ± 0.08 points on MIRAGE-22, and Bernoulli Mask by 1.25 ± 0.16 points on Enterprise. Combining augmentations with MaskedStack reaches a 4.63 ± 0.14-point improvement on MIRAGE-19. (Section 5.1, Table 5; Section 5.4, Table 7)
details.Parameters: The MIRAGE-19 architecture has 115,028 parameters, all trainable. (Appendix, Listing 1.1)
details.Memory: The MIRAGE-19 architecture printout estimates 0.44 MB for parameters, 0.09 MB for the forward/backward pass and 0.53 MB in total. (Appendix, Listing 1.1)
details.Reproducibility: NA — not extracted
details.Deployment limitations: Increasing augmentation injection can make the performance gain too small relative to the computational cost. (Section 5.2, Batching policies)
details.Version notes: A footnote describes a 256-dimensional latent space, but Listing 1.1 shows a 128-channel pooled representation feeding the 20-class linear layer (2,580 parameters). (Section 5.3, footnote 13; Appendix, Listing 1.1)
details.Hardware: Experiments run on Linux servers equipped with multiple NVIDIA Tesla V100 GPUs. (Section 4.1, Model architecture and training)
details.Measurement scope: Memory figures are architecture-printout estimates covering the input, parameters and forward/backward pass. (Appendix, Listing 1.1)

title: Generic Multi-modal Representation Learning for Network Traffic Analysis
summary: Studies reusable representations for traffic analysis.
contribution: Modality adapters and an integration module form multimodal autoencoder embeddings.
limitation: Curator: The reported classification demonstration is narrower than all proposed downstream uses.
gap: Do fixed embeddings transfer across tasks and networks?

details.Research problem: Studies reusable representations for traffic analysis.
details.Traffic unit definition: Samples are TCP/UDP flows for T1 (MIRAGE) and T3 (ISCX) and sender IP addresses for T2 (DARKNET); flow samples use sequences of packet inter-arrival times, lengths and TCP receiver window values, with the first k = 32 measurements in T3. (Section 3.1; Sections 4.1-4.3)
details.Input representation: Bi-modal inputs: entities (server IP addresses, ports, /24 subnets) are embedded with Word2Vec skip-gram, while quantities are adapted per type: flow statistics through a fully connected layer, sequences of quantities through a 1D-CNN, and raw payload bytes through an embedding layer followed by a GRU, each projecting to an l1-dimensional space. (Section 1; Sections 3.2.1-3.2.2)
details.Packets / bytes: T1 flows carry up to 32 bytes of application payload; T3 flows use the first 32 bytes of payload plus statistics from TCP payload; T2 keeps only senders that sent at least five packets in one month. (Sections 4.1-4.3)
details.Preprocessing / anonymisation: MIRAGE background traffic is filtered out in post-processing; ISCX is restricted to non-tunnelled traffic; the DARKNET unknown class is ignored during validation, following the original authors; no IP or port masking is described. (Sections 4.1-4.3; Section 5.1)
details.Architecture: Per-input-type adaptation modules (Word2Vec for entities, FC for statistics, 1D-CNN for sequences, embedding layer plus GRU for payload) feed a symmetric five-layer autoencoder integration module (l2, l3, l4, l3, l2 neurons) whose l4-neuron layer yields the embedding E(s); the downstream classifier is a fully connected feed-forward network with two hidden layers (512 and 256 neurons), 30% dropout, ReLU and Softmax. (Sections 3.2-3.3; Section 5.1)
details.Pretraining objective: Self-supervised reconstruction: the MAE (quantities adaptation modules plus integration module) is trained to minimise a weighted Mean Squared Error reconstruction loss with linear decoder activations; Word2Vec entity embeddings are trained separately with skip-gram, predicting context membership within a window of n words. (Section 3.2.1; Section 3.3)
details.Fine-tuning objective: Supervised downstream traffic classification on frozen MAE embeddings: a fully connected classifier is trained with class-balanced categorical cross-entropy and an Adam optimiser. (Section 5.1)
details.Pretraining datasets: NA — not extracted
details.Training / evaluation datasets: T1: MIRAGE-2019, 44k mobile-app flows, 16 classes, balance 0.94; T2: DARKNET, one month to a /24 darknet, 14k sender IP addresses (5k from known classes), 13 classes plus one unknown, balance 0.4; T3: ISCXVPN2016 non-tunnelled flows, 609 samples, 5 classes, balance 0.82. (Section 4; Table 3)
details.Split strategy: Five-fold cross-validation per task with average statistics reported; stratified sampling for T1 and T3 keeps flows from the same application session on one side of the split; the unknown class is ignored for T2. (Section 5.1)
details.Metrics: Macro average F1-Score and weighted average F1-Score for classification, plus the macro-averaged K-NN class probability pC(K) with cosine distance to gauge embedding neighbourhood purity. (Section 5.2; Section 7.1; Table 4)
details.Reported results: MAE embeddings score 0.87 macro and 0.88 weighted F1 on MIRAGE, 0.98 macro and 1.00 weighted on DARKNET, and 0.68 macro and 0.75 weighted on ISCX, versus 0.89/0.90, 0.98/0.99 and 0.66/0.74 with raw concatenation. Ablations show MAE matches or improves on any single measurement (best individual: 0.82 IP embeddings on T1, 0.98 statistics on T2), and shallow learners on T1 reach 0.86 (RF) and 0.83 (7-NN) macro F1 against the DNN's 0.87. (Table 4; Table 5; Section 8)
details.Parameters: Integration module hidden sizes are fixed at l2 = 512 and l3 = 256 after a coarse grid search, with l4 = 64 (T1) and l1 in [50, 200] for entity embeddings; downstream classifiers need 17 × 10^4 trainable parameters with MAE embeddings versus 29 × 10^4 (T1), 33 × 10^4 (T2) and 28 × 10^4 (T3) with raw concatenation. (Section 5.1; Section 5.2; Section 3.2.1; Table 4)
details.Reproducibility: NA — not extracted
details.Leakage / shortcut risks: Session-level leakage is mitigated for T1 and T3: stratified sampling guarantees flows belonging to the same application session appear only in training or only in testing. (Section 5.1)
details.Deployment limitations: Alternative adaptation and integration architectures (e.g. GNN embeddings) remain untested, and more use cases and datasets are still to be explored. Drift and temporal or spatial generalisation are not investigated, the changing traffic mix alters observable entities and quantities, and privacy-improving techniques and protocols would affect the MAE representations. (Section 9)
details.Version notes: Internal inconsistency: the ISCX IP-address-only macro F1 is 0.46 in the Section 6 text but 0.47 in Table 5; Table 4 omits the T3 reference score because only a fraction of the original ISCX dataset is used. (Section 6; Table 5; Table 4)
details.Measurement scope: The only efficiency-related figure is the number of trainable parameters of downstream classifiers, used as a proxy for training cost; no throughput, latency, memory or FLOPs measurements are reported. (Section 5.2)

details.Research problem: Targets classification under distribution shifts and scarce labels.
details.Traffic unit definition: Multiple flows of a client grouped by flow-level BURST (start-time threshold 1 s) into a traffic relation graph; each flow is a node.

details.Architecture: Vicuna-7B-v1.5 LLM (32 decoder layers) with a flow-graph encoder and structure-aware projector; LLM and graph encoder frozen during instruction tuning.
details.Pretraining objective: Graph structural instruction tuning: traffic graph encoding alignment and self-supervised BURST graph matching, followed by traffic-task instruction tuning.
details.Pretraining datasets: NA — not extracted

details.Split strategy: Shift tasks fine-tune on one time or version and test zero-shot on another; NETD uses 1:3 and 3:1 component ratios and an 80% application subset. Split ratios NA — not reported in reviewed sections.
details.Metrics: Accuracy; macro-averaged precision, recall and F1.

title: MEMENTO: A novel approach for class incremental learning of encrypted traffic
summary: Learns new application classes while retaining old ones.
contribution: Class-incremental fine-tuning with memory, training and rectification components.
limitation: Curator: Learning a scheduled class sequence is not identical to unlabelled concept drift.
gap: How do memory and label budgets trade against forgetting?

details.Research problem: Learns new application classes while retaining old ones.
details.Traffic unit definition: A biflow is a bidirectional flow identified by source and destination IP addresses and ports plus transport protocol, allowing source and destination to be swapped. (Section 4.1, footnote 2)
details.Input representation: Per-packet time series contain transport-layer payload size, inter-arrival time, TCP window size and direction for MIRAGE19; CESNET-TLS22 uses payload size, inter-arrival time and direction because window size is unavailable. (Section 4.1, per-packet properties paragraph)
details.Packets / bytes: Each sample uses the first 10 packets with non-zero payload; shorter sequences are padded with zeros. (Section 4.1, final paragraph)
details.Preprocessing / anonymisation: Zero-payload packets are excluded, direction is encoded by upstream or downstream sign, and UDP window size is set to zero. Memory augmentation applies Gaussian jittering and translation to inter-arrival times. (Sections 4.1 and 3.1.2)
details.Architecture: A 2D-CNN has two convolutional layers followed by pooling and normalisation operations and a dense output layer. The backbone structure stays unchanged while the head expands to accommodate newly added classes. (Section 4.2)
details.Pretraining objective: NA — not extracted
details.Fine-tuning objective: Incremental training combines categorical cross-entropy classification with knowledge distillation from the previous episode, using selective smoothing of teacher responses for new-app samples. A separate correction stage optimises categorical cross-entropy with the main model frozen. (Sections 3.2.1 and 3.3, Equations (1)–(4))
details.Pretraining datasets: NA — not extracted
details.Training / evaluation datasets: MIRAGE19 contains 40 Android app classes; CESNET-TLS22-40 and CESNET-TLS22-80 retain the 40 and 80 most represented services, respectively. CESNET subsets randomly retain 0.15% of biflows per class. (Section 4.1; Tables 4–6 and 8)
details.Split strategy: For balanced incremental validation, stored memory biflows are divided into 90% training and 10% validation, with equal validation counts per class across old and new apps. (Section 3.2.2)
details.Evaluation setting: New-class learning and old-class forgetting relative to retraining.
details.Metrics: Macro F1 and balanced accuracy, defined as mean per-class recall, are reported separately for all, old and new classes. Derived measures are the drop from a model trained from scratch and Maximum Improvement Over the Best Baseline. (Section 4.4, Equations (8)–(11))
details.Reported results: For 39+1, overall macro F1 drops from training from scratch are 2.24 ± 1.02 percentage points on MIRAGE19 and 1.49 ± 0.72 on CESNET-TLS22-40; for 20+20 they are 8.59 ± 1.54 and 6.62 ± 0.66, respectively. On CESNET-TLS22-80, overall drops are 1.34 ± 0.52 for 79+1, 5.87 ± 0.60 for 40+40, and 12.50 ± 0.95 at the final episode of 20+20+20+20. (Tables 4–6 and 8, MEMENTO rows, F1 Score Drop All columns)
details.Reproducibility: NA — not extracted
details.Leakage / shortcut risks: To keep augmented samples within their source partition, each original memory biflow and all its synthetic derivatives are assigned together to training or validation. (Section 6.1, small-increment configuration)
details.Deployment limitations: The performance gap against ideal training from scratch remains. Evaluation in network environments different from training and adaptation to intra-class concept drift are left for future work. (Section 7, final paragraph)
details.Version notes: Section 6.5 claims greater than 90% training-time gain across all datasets in the small-increment scenario, but Table 7 reports 89.38% for MIRAGE19 at 39+1. The classification-loss weight is also inconsistent: Section 4.3 specifies the old-class fraction, whereas Section 5.2 specifies the new-class fraction. (Sections 4.3, 5.2 and 6.5; Table 7)
details.Hardware: Experiments used a machine with two Intel Xeon Gold 6252N CPUs at 2.30 GHz and 378 GB memory; execution-time measurements used a single CPU core. (Section 4; Section 5.1, footnote 5)
details.Measurement scope: Efficiency measurements cover incremental training and post-training herding, using sequential CPU process time in an otherwise idle environment. Table 7 reports training-time reductions against training from scratch, rather than inference performance. (Section 5.1, footnote 5; Section 6.5; Table 7)

title: Benchmarking Class Incremental Learning in Deep Learning Traffic Classification
venue: IEEE Transactions on Network and Service Management
summary: Benchmarks class-incremental traffic learning.
contribution: Systematic comparison of learning new applications without forgetting old ones.
limitation: Curator: Results on one mobile-app corpus do not establish cross-organisation robustness.
gap: Which strategies remain useful with strict retention and labelling budgets?

details.Research problem: Benchmarks class-incremental traffic learning.
details.Traffic unit definition: The traffic unit is a bidirectional flow defined by the transport protocol, source and destination IP addresses, and source and destination ports. (Section V-B, footnote 10)
details.Input representation: Each input is a single-channel matrix containing time series of transport-layer payload size, inter-arrival time, direction and TCP window size. (Sections V-B and V-C)
details.Packets / bytes: Each sample uses the first 10 payload-carrying packets of a biflow, with zero padding for shorter biflows. (Section V-B)
details.Preprocessing / anonymisation: Zero-payload packets are discarded; direction is encoded as upstream or downstream, and the TCP window field is set to zero for UDP packets. (Section V-B; footnote 12)
details.Architecture: The shared backbone has two two-dimensional convolutional layers with 32 and 64 filters of size 4 × 2, each followed by max pooling and batch normalisation. Flattened features feed a fully connected layer of size 200 and an approach-specific output head. (Section V-C; Figure 8)
details.Pretraining objective: NA — not extracted
details.Fine-tuning objective: The authors' iCaRL+ variant combines a classification cross-entropy term over old and new classes with a knowledge-distillation term, and uses the native model head for inference. (Section IV-D; Equations 12 and 17)
details.Pretraining datasets: NA — not extracted
details.Training / evaluation datasets: Evaluation uses MIRAGE19 with 40 Android applications from 16 app-market categories and approximately 100k labelled biflows. (Section V-B)
details.Evaluation setting: FACIL compares LwF, iCaRL, EWC, EEIL, IL2M, LUCIR, BiC and SSIL with iCaRL+, OvA-Ens and six fine-tuning/freezing baselines. Single increments use 20 + 20 and 39 + 1 scenarios; sequential increments start from 20 or 34 applications, with random application orders and a shared CNN backbone. (Sections II, IV, V-C and V-D)
details.Metrics: Metrics are macro F1, DropAll, DropOld and DropNew relative to training from scratch, and Forgetting relative to the best previous performance on old tasks. (Section V-A; Equations 20–22)
details.Reported results: The benchmark finds that BiC and OvA-Ens both exceed 73% macro F1 in the 39 + 1 scenario. High intransigence remains unresolved, with the best reported DropNew still 41.9% in that scenario. (Sections VI-A and VI-E)
details.Parameters: The reference architecture has approximately 540k trainable parameters. (Section V-C)
details.Memory: Exemplar rehearsal normally uses 1k samples; the memory-sensitivity experiment tests budgets of 100, 1k, 10k and 100k samples. (Section V-D; Section VI-C)
details.Reproducibility: NA — not extracted
details.Deployment limitations: OvA-Ens and LUCIR require specially trained base models and cannot extend a conventionally trained classifier. Small increments continue to suffer high intransigence, while the training cost of model-growth approaches limits their use with large increments. (Section VII)
details.Version notes: Online 2023; volume 21(1), 2024. One record for both.
details.Hardware: Controlled timing uses one core of an Intel Core i7-4710MQ CPU at 2.50 GHz with 11.6 GB RAM; an additional comparison uses an NVIDIA Tesla T4 cluster. (Section VI-D, footnote 18)
details.Measurement scope: Efficiency measurements cover CPU process time for model updates, including pre-SGD, SGD and post-SGD operations, and are averaged across runs relative to training from scratch. (Section VI-D; Figure 14; footnotes 18–19)

title: Cross-Network Embeddings Transfer for Traffic Analysis
venue: IEEE Transactions on Network and Service Management
summary: Investigates transferring learned embeddings between networks.
contribution: Domain adaptation with embedding alignment and transfer learning.
limitation: Curator: Representation transfer must be distinguished from training separately on multiple datasets.
gap: What target-domain information is needed to align embeddings?

details.Research problem: Investigates transferring learned embeddings between networks.
details.Traffic unit definition: Packets arriving at darknet or honeypot sensors grouped by destination TCP or UDP port, preserving the sequence of sender hosts contacting each port within a daily window. (Section III-B)
details.Input representation: Continuous vector embeddings in e-dimensional space learned for each host IP address, which serve as inputs to the downstream classifier or aligner neural network. (Section III-B)
details.Packets / bytes: Filtering retains only active hosts that sent at least 5 packets within the one-day collection batch. (Section V-B)
details.Preprocessing / anonymisation: Hosts sending fewer than 5 packets per day are filtered out, and in the honeypot scenario, only TCP-SYN packets are extracted. (Section V-B; Section VII-C)
details.Architecture: The alignment model is a DNN with 3 hidden layers of 1,024 units each with input layer normalisation and linear or Sigmoid activations. The downstream classifier is a feed-forward DNN with two hidden layers of 512 and 256 ReLU units, 30% dropout, and a softmax output layer. (Section IV-B; Section V-C)
details.Pretraining objective: Word2Vec context prediction trained in a self-supervised masked fashion to predict context hosts within a context window cw given a target host in the sequence. (Section III-B)
details.Fine-tuning objective: The aligner DNN is trained to minimise mean squared error between mapped anchor host embeddings, while the downstream classifier minimises categorical cross-entropy using Adam. (Section IV-B; Section V-C)
details.Pretraining datasets: Host embeddings are pretrained on 31 days (December 2022) of packet-level traffic from /24 darknets or 32 days of honeypot traffic. (Section V-B; Section VII-C)
details.Training / evaluation datasets: Two /24 darknet sensors in different autonomous systems and geographic regions captured over 43 days (1 Dec 2022 to 11 Jan 2023) across 10 ground-truth scanner/botnet classes plus unknown, and a 42-day TPOT low-interaction honeypot deployment covering 13 classes. (Section V-B; Section VII-B)
details.Split strategy: Five-fold stratified cross-validation split across provider and customer hosts, structured so that common anchor hosts remain in the same fold; models are trained on 4 provider folds, validated on the 5th provider fold, and tested on the 5th customer fold. (Section VI)
details.Metrics: Macro-averaged precision, recall, and F1-score for supervised classification, and silhouette and homogeneity for unsupervised clustering. (Section VI; Section VIII-A)
details.Reported results: Darknet, both networks with 32 days (Table III): F1 0.92 for canonical transfer (precision 0.94, recall 0.92) and for non-linear alignment (0.96, 0.90), against 0.95 for the independent reference. With 1 customer day (Table II) transfer keeps F1 0.92 against 0.81 for the reference. Honeypot to darknet (Table IV): transfer F1 0.86 (precision and recall 0.88), non-linear alignment 0.80, independent reference 0.81. (Section VI; Tables II–IV)
details.Latency: Per-day i-DarkVec 1-epoch update required 1.7 s on darknet traffic and 23 s on honeypot traffic; per-fold classifier and aligner training averaged 24 s and 60 s to 69 s respectively. (Section V-C; Section VII-C)
details.Reproducibility: NA — not extracted
details.Deployment limitations: The framework requires a non-empty subset of common active senders (anchors) across networks to enable alignment or context transfer, as well as administrative agreements and distribution systems. (Section IV-A; Section VI-C; Section IV-D)
details.Version notes: Early access 2023; journal issue June 2024. Bibliography and institutional abstract reviewed.
details.Hardware: An Nvidia Tesla V100-PCIE-16GB GPU. (Section V-C)
details.Measurement scope: Efficiency measurements encompass the average daily training and update times of i-DarkVec, as well as per-fold training runtimes of the classifier and aligner networks. (Section V-C)

title: Ptu: Pre-Trained Model for Network Traffic Understanding
summary: Unifies static packet content with network dynamics for traffic understanding.
contribution: Self-supervised representation learning over both traffic modalities.
limitation: Curator: Publisher abstract and official conference program establish the model; full dataset and cost tables have not been extracted.
gap: How well does the joint representation transfer to new capture sites?

details.Research problem: Unifies static packet content with network dynamics for traffic understanding.
details.Traffic unit definition: Packet-level: the packet is the input unit and downstream tasks run at the granularity of individual packets, with temporal context drawn from the packet's session flow, the bidirectional stream sharing the protocol, IP and port quintuple. (Section II-A)
details.Input representation: Packet bytes are segmented into 16-bit tokens (vocabulary 2^16 = 65536), while session inter-arrival times normalised by sigmoid(log10(inter-arrival)) form temporal tokens; the modified embedding layer sums token, position, packet and time embeddings, with independent lookup tables for packet versus temporal tokens and [CLS]/[PKT] separators. (Sections II-A, III-B)
details.Packets / bytes: Each sample is one packet truncated to Ni = 128 tokens with at most Nt = 10 appended temporal tokens; pre-training inputs concatenate two packets, and the input sequence length for all experiments is set to 256 bytes. (Sections II-B, III-B, IV-E)
details.Preprocessing / anonymisation: IP addresses, MAC addresses and the checksum field are removed from the otherwise retained network and transport headers to prevent the model learning harmful biases from strong identification fields. (Section II-A)
details.Architecture: Standard BERT backbone with 12 attention heads, 12 layers and 768-dimensional token embeddings; downstream tasks add only a task-specific output layer on the [CLS] token's output vector. (Sections III-A, III-B)
details.Pretraining objective: Four self-supervised targets, Masked Packet Reconstruction, Same Session Prediction, Historical Interval Prediction and Future Interval Prediction, whose losses are summed as the overall pre-training loss. Best settings: Pmasked = 20, Pmask = 80, Prandom = 10, Pnext = 30, Psession = 30, Ptime = 50, run with batch size 32 for 500,000 steps over about five days. (Sections II-B, III-B)
details.Fine-tuning objective: Supervised fine-tuning of the whole pre-trained model on task-specific labelled data, at most 5000 samples per class, with batch size 32 for 10 epochs (about 3 to 10 hours), adding only a task-specific output layer on the [CLS] vector. (Sections III-A, III-B)
details.Pretraining datasets: Approximately 100GB of unlabeled traffic from public datasets [34] and [35], covering QUIC, TLS, FTP, HTTP, SSH and other protocols, both encrypted and plaintext, with no overlap with the labelled evaluation datasets; one shared pre-trained checkpoint serves all downstream tasks. (Section III-B)
details.Training / evaluation datasets: Traffic classification: ISCX-VPN-2016 (application and service), USTC-TFC-2016 (malware), CSTNET-TLS-1.3 (encrypted application), CIC-IoT-2022 (attack) and Cross-Platform iOS and Android (mobile apps). QoE inference: CC-YouTube-QoE-2018 (buffer, resolution, state) plus KoNViD-1k and LIVE Netflix for MOS, where inputs are built from video metadata and features in 100ms slices as in LSTM-QoE. (Section IV-A)
details.Split strategy: Per task, training, validation and test sets are divided 8:1:1; the few-shot analysis deviates from this and varies the training proportion from 10% to 90% in 10% increments. (Sections III-B, IV-D)
details.Metrics: Accuracy and F1 score, macro-averaged over classes to avoid imbalance bias, for traffic and QoE classification tasks; PLCC and SRCC between predicted and actual MOS sequences for the two MOS inference tasks. (Section IV-A)
details.Reported results: PTU is SOTA on all tasks: traffic classification AC and F1 above 0.99 on all six datasets (CSTNET-TLS-1.3 AC 0.9945/F1 0.9940; CIC-IoT-2022 AC 0.9947/F1 0.9942), QoE classification AC 0.9274, 0.9493 and 0.8597 on CC-Buffer, CC-Resolution and CC-State, and MOS PLCC 0.9429 (KoNViD-1k) and 0.9608 (LIVE Netflix). Without pre-training, CSTNET-TLS-1.3 accuracy falls to 0.9132, and PTU stays above 90% accuracy even with 10% of the training data. (Tables II-V; Section IV-D)
details.Latency: An additional delay of approximately 5 ms per flow, which the authors call non-negligible. (Section VI)
details.Throughput: Offline batch inference: about 200 samples per second at batch size 1 with 256-byte inputs, and approximately 3000 samples per second at batch size 32 (the experimental default); linear attention could add a further 3 to 4 times speed-up but degrades performance. (Section IV-E)
details.Reproducibility: NA — not extracted
details.Leakage / shortcut risks: IP and MAC addresses are removed to prevent harmful biases from strong identification fields; the 'w IP' ablation shows retaining them costs only moderate accuracy because IP addresses correlate consistently with labels within each dataset's train and test subsets, a shortcut expected to cause more pronounced degradation in production. Pre-training and evaluation datasets are stated to have no overlap. (Sections II-A, III-B, IV-C)
details.Deployment limitations: The authors state the roughly 2000 samples per second inference speed lags the core network requirement of tens of millions of packets per second, that the 5 ms per-flow delay is non-negligible, and that applying PTU to the real-world core network is still challenging. (Section VI)
details.Version notes: Section IV-E reports approximately 3000 samples per second at batch size 32 whereas Section VI reports approximately 2000 samples per second on a single consumer-grade GPU; Table V labels the MPR ablation row 'w/o MTM' while the text calls it 'w/o MPR'. (Sections IV-E, VI; Table V)
details.Hardware: All experiments ran on a server with NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3090 GPUs, four for pre-training and a single GPU for fine-tuning; implementation uses Uer-py and PyTorch 2.1.2. (Section III-B)
details.Measurement scope: The efficiency numbers cover offline batch inference on an RTX 3090 with 256-byte inputs at batch sizes 1 and 32 only; they do not cover live core-network operation, which the authors state PTU cannot yet meet. (Sections IV-E, VI)

title: ExpMD: an Explainable Framework for Traffic Identification Based on Multi-Domain Features
summary: Makes traffic-identification decisions inspectable across multiple feature domains.
contribution: Multi-domain feature representation with an explanation framework.
limitation: Curator: Explanations expose model dependence without proving causal or cross-network robustness.
gap: Do the explanations remain stable under capture shift and feature removal?

details.Research problem: Makes traffic-identification decisions inspectable across multiple feature domains.
details.Traffic unit definition: Flow defined by 5-tuple (source IP, destination IP, source port, destination port, and protocol), encompassing both upload and download directions. (Section III)
details.Input representation: Four domains: metadata features (packet counts, byte counts, flow duration), byte-distribution domain (concatenated 256-dimensional byte frequency vectors for upload and download), textual domain (raw byte sequences mapped via byte embeddings), and temporal domain (signed packet lengths mapped to [-MTU, +MTU] and converted via an embedding layer). (Section III; Section IV-A to IV-D)
details.Packets / bytes: First 784 bytes of upload payload and first 784 bytes of download payload, padded with [PAD] when shorter; packet lengths capped at MTU of 1500. (Section IV-C; Section IV-D)
details.Architecture: ExpMD ensembles four sub-models via soft voting: Meta-RF (Random Forest), BD-boost (XGBoost on 512-dimensional vector), Text-Net (byte embedding, 1D-CNN pooling, L-layer residual blocks for upload and download processed separately and merged via MLP), and PS-Net (bidirectional multi-layer RNN over packet-length embeddings merged via MLP). (Section IV-A to IV-E; Fig. 1; Fig. 2; Fig. 3)
details.Pretraining objective: NA — not extracted
details.Fine-tuning objective: Cross-entropy loss for Text-Net; weighted multi-task objective combining cross-entropy loss and Triplet loss for PS-Net. (Section IV-C; Section IV-D)
details.Pretraining datasets: NA — not extracted
details.Training / evaluation datasets: NUDT_MobileTraffic dataset, using 104 selected applications divided into a training dataset and a testing dataset. (Section V)
details.Evaluation setting: Traffic identification; full dataset inventory NA — not extracted.
details.Metrics: Accuracy, macro-F1, and class counts/percentages exceeding specified F1 score thresholds. (Section V-A; Table II; Table III)
details.Reported results: ExpMD achieves an accuracy of 0.9755 (97.5%) and macro-F1 of 0.9756 across 104 applications. Sub-models achieve: Meta-RF (accuracy 0.8927, macro-F1 0.8921), BD-boost (accuracy 0.9103, macro-F1 0.9111), Text-Net (accuracy 0.9508, macro-F1 0.9517), and PS-Net (accuracy 0.9053, macro-F1 0.9055). (Abstract; Section V-A; Table II)
details.Reproducibility: NA — not extracted
details.Deployment limitations: Removal or obfuscation of plaintext initial handshake metadata (such as TLS SNI) significantly degrades textual-domain performance, byte-distribution features offer limited signal under uniform encryption payloads, and behavioral features in metadata and temporal domains carry higher risk of confusion across similar behaviors. (Section VI)

details.Hardware: Server with Intel Xeon Gold 5222 CPU @ 3.80GHz, NVIDIA GeForce GTX 3090 GPU, and 128GB of RAM. (Section V)

title: Mean Masked Autoencoder with Flow-Mixing for Encrypted Traffic Classification
summary: Learns byte, packet and flow context through self-distillation.
contribution: Teacher–student masked autoencoder with cross-flow mixing and packet-aware masking.
limitation: Curator: Packet sizes and timing guide masking; pretraining is memory intensive and classification was evaluated on the paper’s splits.
gap: Does its gain survive capture-disjoint tests and deliberate timing perturbations?
